WHY: A small, highly compressed image with huge pixel dimensions (a decompression bomb) makes each convert run allocate gigabytes and burn CPU, which ties up web/defer workers. HOW: Check pixel dimensions (e.g. FastImage.size) before downsizing and reject images above a sane limit.

WHAT: The client-side size check now uses a hardcoded 10MB for every upload type, attachments included, instead of `max_<type>_size_kb`. WHY: Sites with max_attachment_size_kb above 10MB now see larger attachments rejected in the browser, and the error message reports the wrong limit for attachments. HOW: Keep the hardcoded 10MB only for images and keep using the site setting for other types.

Ruby has no method overloading, so the second `self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` replaces the `(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` version. `ResizeEmoji` calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 100, opts)` with 5 arguments and now gets an ArgumentError, so emoji resizing breaks. Use one method that accepts both forms, or give the dimensions-string variant a different name.

Ruby has no overloading, so `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` replaces the `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` definition just above it. app/jobs/regular/resize_emoji.rb:14 still calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 100, opts)` with 5 arguments, which now raises ArgumentError, so emoji resizing breaks. Merge the two into one method that accepts both forms, or update the emoji job to pass "100x100".

Ruby keeps only the last `def self.downsize`, so the `(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` version is silently overwritten by `(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`. The existing call in app/jobs/regular/resize_emoji.rb:14 (`OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 100, opts)`) now raises ArgumentError (5 for 3..4), so emoji resizing breaks. Combine the two into one method that accepts both call styles, or give the new one a different name.

The client size check now uses a fixed 10MB limit for every upload type, including attachments, instead of `max_attachment_size_kb`. If that setting is above 10MB, the browser rejects attachments the server would accept. Only image uploads, which the server can now shrink, should get the larger client-side limit.

The new 3-argument `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts)` was added so uploads_controller can pass "80%", but Ruby has no overloading, so it replaces the 4-argument `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts)` defined just above it. As a result, `ResizeEmoji` (`OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 100, opts)`) now raises ArgumentError because it passes 5 arguments to a method that accepts 3–4. Keep one `downsize` that accepts both call shapes, or give the new form a different name and use that name in the controller.

The size check and the `file_too_large` message now use a hard-coded 10MB for every upload type. The server still enforces `max_attachment_size_kb` for attachments (site_settings.yml:516). So users see a max size that doesn't match the limit actually applied, and an attachment the client accepts can still be rejected by the server. Keep using `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` for attachments, and only raise the client limit for images, which the server now downsizes.

A 413 response comes from the web server's client_max_body_size. The site setting descriptions tell admins to keep that value in sync with the max_*_size_kb settings, and it has nothing to do with a fixed 10MB. Hard-coding 10 * 1024 here means the alert can tell users the wrong maximum size whenever the real limit differs.

The comment says large images 'will be automatically reduced to allowed size'. The loop stops after 5 downsizes to 80% without checking whether the file is now under max_image_size_kb, and it ignores the return value of downsize. Either reword the comment to say this is a best-effort reduction, or make the code guarantee the result.

issues.descricao: downsize is defined twice in OptimizedImage; the new (from, to, dimensions, opts) version overrides the (max_width, max_height) one, so existing callers such as ResizeEmoji that pass width and height now raise ArgumentError.
issues.textoGolden: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: A second `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` is defined that overrides the existing `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at lines 145-147. WHY: Ruby uses the last definition, so the effective downsize now only accepts 3-4 args, and the existing caller app/jobs/regular/resize_emoji.rb:14 (`OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 100, opts)`) passes 5 args and raises ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments, given 5, expected 3..4), breaking emoji resizing. HOW: Remove the duplicate; keep a single downsize method whose signature matches all callers (the 4-arg uploads_controller call `downsize(path, path, "80%", allow_animation: ...)` and the 5-arg ResizeEmoji call), or rename one of them.

`downsize` is defined twice: the original 5-param form `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts)` at lines 145-147 and the new 4-param form `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts)` at lines 149-151. Ruby keeps only the last definition, so the effective signature is now 4 params and the 5-param version is dead code. The pre-existing consumer app/jobs/regular/resize_emoji.rb:14 still calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 100, opts)` with 5 positional args, which now raises ArgumentError on every emoji resize. Either update that caller to the new `dimensions` form or remove the redundant override so the old signature keeps working.

`self.downsize` is defined twice in the same class scope (line 145 `(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` and the new line 149 `(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`). Ruby keeps only the last definition, so the 4-argument version is dead and unreachable. The existing caller `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 100, opts)` in app/jobs/regular/resize_emoji.rb:14 passes 5 arguments and will now raise ArgumentError (expected 3..4). Remove the duplicate definition (keep only the `dimensions`-based one, or convert resize_emoji's call), otherwise emoji resizing breaks.

issues.descricao: The client-side upload size check hardcodes 10 MB instead of the per-type max_<type>_size_kb setting, so attachment limits diverge from the server: larger allowed attachments are blocked and smaller limits are only enforced server-side.
issues.textoGolden: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).

comentarios.texto: Hardcoded max size literal 10 * 1024 replaces site-setting-derived max size. Behavioral concern outside assigned class.

The fixed 10 MB client limit is applied to attachments as well as images, replacing max_attachment_size_kb. Sites configured to allow attachments larger than 10 MB can no longer upload those valid files through the composer, although UploadValidator still permits them. Apply the new input ceiling only to images and retain the configured attachment limit.

WHAT: Client check hardcodes maxSizeKB to 10*1024 instead of Discourse.SiteSettings['max_'+type+'_size_kb'], losing image vs attachment distinction. WHY: Sites with smaller max_attachment_size_kb pass client validation then fail server-side, and sites with limits >10MB incorrectly block valid uploads with wrong max_size_kb message. HOW: Restore per-type SiteSetting lookup (keep 10MB only as image downsize ceiling).

issues.descricao: The upload downsizing passes a percentage ('80%') as dimensions, but for animated GIFs the gifsicle path uses --resize-fit, which expects WxH geometry, so downsizing silently fails.
issues.textoGolden: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.

comentarios.texto: The controller passes the percentage string `"80%"` as the dimensions argument to `OptimizedImage.downsize`, but the consumer requires explicit `WxH` geometry: the code this PR deleted built exactly `"#{width}x#{height}"`, and the animated path runs `gifsicle --resize-fit #{dimensions}`, which rejects a percentage. Pass an explicit size (e.g. a computed `"WxH"` from the max KB target) so the auto-downsize actually reduces the file, rather than silently no-oping and leaving oversized uploads.

Caller passes "80%" as dimensions to OptimizedImage.downsize, but the downsize/optimize instruction builders in optimized_image.rb expect explicit "WxH" geometry (interpolated as -resize #{dimensions}\>). A bare percentage does not satisfy that contract and will produce a malformed geometry. Fix the caller to supply WxH dimensions or add explicit percentage handling to the callee.

issues.descricao: Auto-downsizing passes the upload tempfile path, which lacks a .gif extension, so the animated branch is never chosen and convert keeps only the first frame, flattening oversized animated GIFs.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The new auto-downsize call passes a tempfile path whose name has no `.GIF` extension, so `optimize` never selects the animated branch (`method_name += "_animated" if opts[:allow_animation] && from =~ /\.GIF$/i`) and uses `downsize_instructions`, which runs `convert from[0]` and keeps only the first frame. WHY: Animated GIFs larger than max_image_size_kb that are uploaded through this path have their animation flattened to a single frame even though SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails is enabled. HOW: Detect the image type from the original filename/content-type rather than the tempfile path (or pass a flag) so the gifsicle animated downsize path is used for GIF inputs.

Passing the multipart tempfile path to downsize prevents animation detection when that path does not end in .gif, even when allow_animated_thumbnails is enabled. OptimizedImage.optimize checks the path suffix and otherwise uses convert with input[0], so oversized animated GIF uploads are permanently flattened to their first frame. Preserve the original image extension in the processing path or pass the image format explicitly to select animated processing.

issues.descricao: The comment promises images are reduced to the allowed size, but the loop only tries five 80% reductions with no guarantee of reaching the limit.

comentarios.texto: The comment says large images are "automatically reduced to allowed size", but the loop only resizes by 80% up to 5 attempts (≈0.33× of the original in the best case) and then stops without any check that the result actually meets `max_image_size_kb`. The prose promises a guarantee the code does not provide; either make the loop actually converge to the allowed size or reword the comment to state that the image is only attempted to be reduced.

issues.descricao: The downsize retry loop ignores the false return of a failed conversion and repeats the same failing ImageMagick call up to five times.

comentarios.texto: The retry loop ignores downsize's false return value and retries failed conversions while the file remains oversized. convert_with returns false on converter failure, so an unsupported or malformed oversized image launches the same failing external conversion up to five times per upload without any changed input. Break on a failed downsize result and return an upload error rather than repeating the conversion.

WHAT: Downsize loop ignores OptimizedImage.downsize return value and retries up to 5 times unconditionally while checking tempfile.size. WHY: Failed converts (e.g. SVG, invalid 80%> geometry, corrupt image) burn 5 ImageMagick runs then Upload.create_for still runs with oversized/unmodified file and fails validation, wasting CPU and breaking the feature. HOW: Break on false return and handle failure.

issues.descricao: Claims up to five synchronous ImageMagick runs per oversized upload block request threads and enable DoS.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Up to 5 synchronous OptimizedImage.downsize + ImageOptim convert runs execute inline in create_upload request cycle for every oversized image. WHY: Blocks the Rails request thread with CPU-intensive shell-outs per upload, enabling easy request-thread exhaustion/DoS with large images. HOW: Move downsizing to background job or enforce single-pass/timeout.

issues.descricao: Claims the downsize loop checking tempfile.size may never terminate because of a stale cached size, causing infinite loops.
issues.textoGolden: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

issues.descricao: The 413 upload error message states a hard-coded 10 MB maximum that may not match the limit the server or web server actually enforces.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: `group.users.delete(user_id)` on a has_many :through removes the GroupUser row with delete_all semantics, so GroupUser callbacks (the `counter_cache: "user_count"` decrement) do not run, and the user's primary_group_id is not cleared. WHY: groups.user_count stays inflated after removals, so the admin list shows the wrong count. Removed users also keep this group as their primary group (title/flair) even though they are no longer members. HOW: destroy the join record and clear primary_group_id, as destroy_deletions does.

WHAT: add_members calls group.add(user) (users.push) for every username without checking whether the user is already a member. WHY: group_users has a UNIQUE (group_id,user_id) index, so adding an existing member raises ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique and returns a 500, while users earlier in the list stay inserted (partial update). HOW: skip users who are already members.

WHAT: totalPages uses Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1, which counts one page too many whenever user_count is an exact multiple of limit (for example 50 users with limit 50 gives 2 pages). WHY: showingLast stays false on the real last page, so 'next' moves offset to user_count and loads an empty member page labeled 2/2. HOW: use Math.ceil.

WHAT: the public members endpoint takes limit straight from params with no upper bound or positivity check. WHY: any visitor can request limit=1000000 and force serialization of every member of large groups, including automatic trust-level groups. A negative limit produces a PostgreSQL error (500). HOW: clamp limit to a sane range.

`floor(user_count / limit) + 1` gives one page too many when user_count is an exact multiple of limit. For example, 50 members with a limit of 50 shows "1/2", and clicking next loads an empty page at offset 50. Use `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` to get the real page count.

`Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` adds an extra page whenever user_count is an exact multiple of limit (e.g. 50 users with limit 50 gives 2 pages). As a result `showingLast` is false on the real last page, and `next` moves the offset to user_count and loads an empty members page. Use `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` instead.

floor(user_count / limit) + 1 gives one page too many when user_count divides evenly by limit (e.g. 50 members, limit 50 → 2 pages). As a result, showingLast is false on the real last page, and 'next' loads an empty page shown as 2/2. Use Math.ceil(user_count / limit) instead.

This test sends `xhr :put` to remove_member, but in routes.rb remove_member is reachable only through `delete "members"`; PUT on that path goes to add_members. Controller specs skip verb routing, so the test exercises a request the app never routes to this action and would not catch a broken DELETE mapping. Use `xhr :delete` here so it matches the real endpoint and the sibling success test.

The members endpoint used to return every member of a non-automatic group, and now it always applies `limit` (default 50). The public group members page (`group-members.js.es6` / `group/members.hbs`) calls `findMembers()` once and has no paging controls, so any member past the 50th can no longer be reached there. Either add next/previous paging to the public page, or keep returning the full list to callers that don't send a limit.

issues.descricao: The admin group pager computes total pages as floor(user_count / limit) + 1, so when the member count is an exact multiple of the limit it shows an extra page and Next navigates to an empty member list.
issues.textoGolden: The `totalPages` calculation using `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` produces an extra page when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`, leading to incorrect pagination. For example, with 100 users and a limit of 50, it reports 3 pages instead of 2, allowing navigation to an empty page.

comentarios.texto: totalPages (and currentPage) use `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`, which is an off-by-one when user_count is an exact multiple of limit (e.g. 50 members, limit 50 → reports 2 pages although only 1 exists). This leaves `showingLast` false on the real last page, so 'next' navigates to an empty page at offset=user_count. Use `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` (and compute currentPage consistently) to get the correct page count.

totalPages is off by one when user_count is an exact multiple of limit: `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` gives 2 for user_count=50, limit=50, although 50 members occupy exactly one page. Correct it to `Math.ceil(this.get('user_count') / this.get('limit'))`. Effect: for a group whose member count is a multiple of the page size, totalPages is one too high, showingLast remains false so the 'next' link stays enabled, and clicking it navigates to a phantom empty page.

`totalPages` uses `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`, which over-counts by one whenever `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit` (e.g. 50 members with limit 50 yields 2 pages instead of 1). Since `showingLast` is `propertyEqual("currentPage", "totalPages")`, on a full last page `showingLast` is false, so the `next` action stays enabled and advances `offset` to `user_count`, rendering an empty page labeled as the last page. Use `Math.ceil(user_count / limit)` (with the zero-member guard) so the count matches the real number of pages.

issues.descricao: Several Group model functions (findMembers, destroy, userCountDisplay) return a value on some paths and undefined on others, triggering consistent-return lint warnings.
issues.textoGolden: Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

issues.descricao: Paging actions fire overlapping member requests and each response unconditionally overwrites offset and members, so a stale response arriving last can revert the list to an earlier page.

comentarios.texto: Guard against stale member-fetch responses before updating the model. `next` updates offset immediately and leaves navigation enabled, so with at least three pages two rapid clicks issue requests for offsets 50 and 100. If the offset-100 response arrives first and the offset-50 response arrives last, this unconditional `setProperties` resets both offset and members to the older page, undoing the latest navigation. Refreshes after membership changes can similarly be overwritten by an earlier fetch. Track a per-model request generation and apply only the latest response, or serialize navigation and refresh requests.

issues.descricao: The public members endpoint now always caps results at 50 per page, but the public group members page has no pagination, so groups with more than 50 members are silently truncated for users.

comentarios.texto: The public members route now loads only the model's default 50-member page without providing any way to request subsequent pages. The public group/members.hbs template only renders members and has no Next/Previous controls, so members after the first 50 become inaccessible (manual groups previously returned all members). Add public pagination controls and actions that update offset and reload members.

The new default limit applies to nonautomatic groups as well, but the public group-members route still calls findMembers() only once and its template simply iterates members without pagination. Previously this endpoint returned every member of a nonautomatic group; now a group with more than 50 members exposes only the first 50 on its public members page, with no way to reach the rest. Update that consumer to fetch subsequent pages or provide pagination when introducing this endpoint contract.

Provide pagination or load subsequent pages for the public group-members view. findMembers now requests only 50 members, and this route calls it only once while its template simply iterates members without navigation. Custom groups previously returned all members, so groups larger than 50 now have members that cannot be viewed on this page.

issues.descricao: Creating a group ignores the alias_level the admin selected, saving only name and visibility, so new groups keep the default alias level.

comentarios.texto: Persist params[:alias_level] when creating a group, just as update does. The creation form exposes aliasLevelOptions and group.asJSON sends the selected alias_level, but create saves only name and visible. A newly created group therefore retains the default alias level instead of the administrator's selection.

issues.descricao: Removing a member deletes the membership row directly and skips clearing the user's primary_group_id, so a removed user can keep this group as their primary group.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: remove_member uses group.users.delete(user_id) instead of the Group#remove destroy path. WHY: bypasses GroupUser destroy callbacks and primary_group_id cleanup done in destroy_deletions, leaving stale membership side-effects (e.g. dangling primary_group_id). HOW: load the User and call group.remove(user).

Removing a member with group.users.delete bypasses the primary_group_id cleanup previously performed by Group#destroy_deletions during usernames updates. A user whose primary group is this group remains associated with it as their primary group after membership removal, leaving stale primary-group state used by user administration and post serialization. Clear primary_group_id for the removed user when it equals this group's id as part of the removal operation.

issues.descricao: The remove_member spec issues a PUT request although the route only maps DELETE to remove_member, so the test uses a verb never routed in production.
issues.textoGolden: The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.

comentarios.texto: This example sends `xhr :put, :remove_member`, but the PR maps `remove_member` only to DELETE (`delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"`); PUT on that path routes to `groups#add_members`. Controller specs bypass the router, so the example still lands on `remove_member` and passes regardless — it would still pass if the DELETE route were missing or wired to the wrong action, leaving the newly introduced verb/action pairing untested. Use `xhr :delete, :remove_member`, as the sibling example at line 125 already does.

The test 'cannot remove members from automatic groups' sends `xhr :put, :remove_member`, but the route is `delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"`. It exercises the action with a verb that is never routed in production. Use `xhr :delete, :remove_member, group_id: 1, user_id: 42` so the test matches the real request.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: The fallback locales are only loaded by FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!, and only ApplicationController calls it; I18n.translate loads just config.locale. WHY: Code that switches locale outside the controller (PostAlerter's I18n.with_locale(user.effective_locale), Jobs::Base, PostDestroyer, JsLocaleHelper) falls back to :en or the site locale even when that locale was never loaded, so it returns 'translation missing' instead of the fallback text. HOW: Load the whole fallback chain where translation happens, e.g. in I18n.translate call `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` (or load each locale from `fallbacks[config.locale]`) instead of loading only config.locale.

WHAT: The fallback chain now depends on SiteSetting.default_locale, but the translate LRU cache key is still only key+locale+backend id. WHY: A result computed before a fallback locale was loaded ('translation missing'), or before an admin changed default_locale, stays frozen in the cache and keeps being served. HOW: Add the fallback chain to the cache key, e.g. include `SiteSetting.default_locale` in `k`, or clear `@cache` when default_locale changes.

`I18n.fallbacks` now sends lookups to the site default locale and to :en, but `translate` still loads only `config.locale`. The fallback locales are loaded only by the new `ensure_loaded!` call in ApplicationController. Translations made outside a controller request (jobs, mailers, console) therefore fall back to locales that were never loaded, and the LRU cache stores the resulting "translation missing" string, so `translate` should load every locale in the fallback chain.

Fallback locales (site default, :en) are loaded only by the new `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` in ApplicationController, while `translate` still loads only `config.locale`. In Sidekiq jobs, mailers or rake tasks, a key missing in the user's locale falls back to a locale that was never loaded, and the resulting "translation missing" string is frozen into the LRU cache under the real key, so it keeps being returned after the fallback locale loads. Load the fallback chain inside `translate` (or `load_locale`) itself, not only in the controller.

With I18n::Backend::Fallbacks enabled, lookups now also read SiteSetting.default_locale and :en, but `translate` still only calls load_locale(config.locale). The fallback locales are loaded only by `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` in ApplicationController#set_locale. In jobs, mailers and rake tasks the fallback chain therefore points at locales that were never loaded, and missing keys come back as 'translation missing' instead of the English text; to fix this, have translate load every locale in I18n.fallbacks[config.locale].

The new Fallbacks backend in config/initializers/i18n.rb looks up keys in the site default locale and in :en, but `translate` only lazy-loads `config.locale`. The fallback locales are loaded only when ApplicationController calls `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!`, so translations in jobs, mailers or other non-controller code fall back to unloaded locales and return 'translation missing', and the cache keeps that result. Load the whole fallback chain inside `translate`, for example by replacing the single `load_locale(config.locale)` with `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!`.

issues.descricao: Fallback locale catalogs are only loaded in the controller's set_locale filter, while translate loads just the current locale, so translations outside requests (jobs, mailers) cannot fall back to the site default or English.

comentarios.texto: Fallback catalogs are ensured loaded only in the controller filter, leaving non-controller translation paths without the catalogs required by the newly enabled fallback backend. Jobs::Base sets I18n.locale directly and PostAlerter uses I18n.with_locale, while the accelerator loads only the current locale and backend fallback lookups bypass that loader; missing keys therefore still produce missing translations or skip the configured site fallback until another request happens to load those catalogs. Ensure the full fallback chain is loaded at the translation boundary, rather than relying solely on the controller filter.

The new fallbacks contract requires the fallback locales (site default and :en, from FallbackLocaleList#[]) to be loaded before Backend::Simple#translate is asked for them — Backend::Simple only returns already-loaded translations. This PR added I18n.ensure_loaded!/I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! but wired it only into ApplicationController#set_locale, and the loader that actually gates every translation, I18n.translate (line 68), still loads only `config.locale`. As a result, any I18n.t performed outside the request cycle (console, background jobs, mailers) or before set_locale runs will not load the fallback locales and will silently return 'translation missing' instead of the fallback the new I18n.fallbacks advertises. Fix: have translate ensure the fallback chain is loaded (e.g. call I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! / load the fallback locales here), not rely on the controller hook.

translate loads only config.locale, but the new fallback chain (default_locale, :en) is loaded only by the controller's I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!. Outside controllers (jobs, mailers, rake), a key missing in the current locale falls back to a locale that is not loaded, so it returns 'translation missing', and the LRU cache then stores that result. Fix: in translate, call I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! (or load each locale in fallbacks[config.locale]) before the lookup.

issues.descricao: The translation cache key does not include the site or its default locale, but fallback results now depend on SiteSetting.default_locale, so multisite processes or a changed default locale serve stale fallback translations.

comentarios.texto: The new fallback order depends on SiteSetting.default_locale, but the accelerator's translation cache does not include that setting or the current site in its key. In a multisite process, two sites with the same user locale and different default locales reuse the first site's cached fallback translation; changing the default locale also leaves cached fallback results stale. Include the effective fallback chain or site/default-locale context in the translation cache key.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: ProvideAnonDBStore now takes an int64 deviceLimit, but pkg/server/wire.go:374-375 still registers it as a provider and binds anonstore.AnonStore to it. WHY: Wire has no provider for int64, so DI generation fails and the server won't build. The store is also no longer injected anywhere. HOW: Remove anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore and its wire.Bind from wire.go, or have the provider take *setting.Cfg and read AnonymousDeviceLimit from it.

WHAT: TagDevice now returns ErrDeviceLimitReached to block authentication, but tagDeviceUI writes the device's localCache key before CreateOrUpdateDevice runs and leaves it there when the call fails. WHY: Only the first request from a device over the limit is rejected; for the next 29 minutes the cache hit returns nil and the request is authenticated anonymously, so the limit is effectively not enforced. HOW: In tagDeviceUI, set the cache entry only after CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds, or delete it when the call fails.

WHAT: Authenticate enforces the device limit only through TagDevice, and TagDevice returns nil when the client-controlled X-Grafana-Device-Id header is empty (impl.go:119-122). WHY: Any client that leaves out the header, or sends a fresh random ID each time, gets an anonymous identity no matter what device_limit is set to. HOW: When a device limit is configured, reject anonymous authentication for requests without a device ID.

WHAT: updateDevice treats RowsAffected()==0 as ErrDeviceLimitReached, but MySQL by default reports changed rows, not matched rows. WHY: When the limit is reached, an already-registered device whose client_ip, user_agent and second-precision updated_at are unchanged (for example, concurrent requests across instances) gets 0 rows and is wrongly denied. HOW: Check that the device exists with a SELECT on device_id within the window instead of relying on RowsAffected.

WHAT: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices and then inserts without a transaction, lock or constraint. WHY: Concurrent requests from new devices can all see count < deviceLimit before any of them inserts, so the configured limit is exceeded. HOW: Run the count and insert in one transaction with appropriate locking, or do a conditional insert that checks the count in the same statement.

WHAT: Device tagging used to run in a background goroutine with its own timeout and now runs inline in Authenticate. With a limit set, that means a COUNT(*) over anon_device plus an upsert for every uncached device. WHY: Anonymous authentication now waits on these DB round trips, so a slow DB or a flood of new device IDs adds latency and DB load to every such anonymous request. HOW: Keep the DB write async and enforce the limit from a cached or periodically refreshed device count.

The doc comment says `updateDevice` updates a device "updated between the given times", but it takes only ctx and device. It computes the window internally as `device.UpdatedAt` minus 30 days to `device.UpdatedAt` plus one minute, and returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` when no row matches, so callers reading the comment get the wrong contract.

ProvideAnonDBStore now takes a `deviceLimit int64` parameter, but pkg/server/wire.go:374-375 still lists `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` as a provider and binds `anonstore.AnonStore` to it. Wire cannot supply a bare int64, so dependency-injection generation/build fails. AnonDeviceService now builds the store itself, so remove the provider and the Bind from wire.go.

The device count and the insert/upsert run as separate statements with no transaction or lock. Concurrent requests from new devices can all read count < deviceLimit and all insert, so the limit is exceeded. Make the check and the insert one atomic operation, for example a conditional insert or a locked transaction.

tagDeviceUI puts the device key in localCache before CreateOrUpdateDevice runs and returns nil early on a cache hit. When the limit is reached, only the first request gets ErrDeviceLimitReached, and requests from the same device in the next 29 minutes skip the DB check and authenticate. Set the cache entry only after the store write succeeds.

tagDeviceUI caches the device key before CreateOrUpdateDevice, and the key stays cached when that call returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Now that this error rejects authentication, only the first request from a device over the limit is denied. Its later requests within the 29-minute cache TTL get nil back from tagDeviceUI and are authenticated, so the limit is not enforced. Fix: delete the cache entry when CreateOrUpdateDevice fails, or set it only after the call succeeds.

`pkg/server/wire.go:374-375` still registers `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` and binds `AnonStore` to it. The new signature needs an `int64` that no wire provider supplies, and after the change to `impl.go` nothing consumes `AnonStore`, so the provider is also unused. Wire generation fails. Remove the provider and its binding from `wire.go`, or give the provider an injectable dependency such as `*setting.Cfg`.

This check assumes `TagDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` on every request from a device over the limit. But `tagDeviceUI` in `impl.go` puts the device key in `localCache` before `CreateOrUpdateDevice` fails, so for the next 29 minutes later requests hit the cache, get nil, and are authenticated. Write the cache entry only after the store write succeeds, or remove the key when the limit is hit.

issues.descricao: The device limit check counts devices and then inserts in separate non-atomic steps, so concurrent requests from new devices can all pass the check and exceed the configured limit.
issues.textoGolden: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.

comentarios.texto: The limit check counts devices and then inserts in separate steps with no lock or transaction. Concurrent requests from new devices can all see count < limit and all insert, so the limit is exceeded. Make the count-and-insert atomic, for example with a conditional INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*)) < limit.

The device limit check is a non-atomic count followed by an insert. Concurrent requests from different new devices can all see count < limit and all insert, so the number of devices exceeds deviceLimit. Make the check and insert atomic, for example with a conditional INSERT ... SELECT WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*)) < limit, or serialize the check and insert under a lock.

WHAT: CreateOrUpdateDevice does check-then-act (CountDevices then INSERT/UPSERT) with no lock, transaction, or unique-guard when deviceLimit>0. WHY: Two concurrent new-device requests can both observe count < limit and both insert, exceeding the configured limit and breaking the enforcement contract. HOW: Enforce atomically (e.g., conditional insert guarded by count in one statement/transaction with serializable lock, or re-check count on conflict).

issues.descricao: Device slots are keyed by the client-controlled X-Grafana-Device-Id header with no validation or rate limiting, so an anonymous caller can fill the limit with fake IDs and deny anonymous access to every new legitimate device.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Device slots counted toward deviceLimit are keyed by the unauthenticated X-Grafana-Device-Id header (read in impl.go TagDevice) with no validation or rate-limit. WHY: Any anonymous caller can mint arbitrary device IDs to fill the table up to the limit, after which all legitimate new anonymous devices get ErrDeviceLimitReached and authentication is denied — a trivial anonymous-access DoS introduced by the limit. HOW: Do not let a single client consume many slots (e.g., bind slot consumption to IP/fingerprint, rate-limit new-device creation, or require proof of distinct device).

issues.descricao: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only checks that a new device is rejected at the limit and never verifies that an existing device can still be updated at the limit.

comentarios.texto: The at-limit call reuses a brand-new device ID ("keep") that was never inserted, so it only reaches updateDevice's `rowsAffected == 0` -> ErrDeviceLimitReached branch. The success branch of the newly added updateDevice (an existing device still being updated while the store is at the limit) is never exercised by any test — every other call uses deviceLimit 0, so updateDevice is never invoked. A regression that made updateDevice always affect 0 rows, use a wrong WHERE/SET, or unconditionally return ErrDeviceLimitReached whenever limit>0 would leave this and all other tests green. Add a case that, after the store is at the limit, calls CreateOrUpdateDevice again with the SAME DeviceID and asserts require.NoError (and ideally that client_ip/user_agent/updated_at were changed), so the update path is actually verified.

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only checks that a new device is rejected at the limit. It would still pass if updateDevice always returned ErrDeviceLimitReached, because it never re-submits the existing device (DeviceID "32mdo31deeqwes") at the limit. Add a call that updates the existing device with a new UserAgent or UpdatedAt, require NoError, and check the stored row changed.

issues.descricao: tagDeviceUI caches the device key before CreateOrUpdateDevice; when the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached the entry stays, so the next request from the same device skips the limit check and authenticates for up to 29 minutes.
issues.textoGolden: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: TagDevice failures that triggered the new ErrDeviceLimitReached early-return are not permanent, because tagDeviceUI (impl.go:87) writes the device key into localCache BEFORE CreateOrUpdateDevice (impl.go:93) and never evicts it on error; tagDeviceUI returns early on any cache hit (impl.go:83-84). WHY: the first request from a new over-limit device is denied, but the poisoned cache makes every subsequent request from that same device skip the limit check entirely and authenticate successfully, so the configurable device limit is bypassed by simply retrying. HOW: only set the cache key after CreateOrUpdateDevice returns nil (e.g. move a.localCache.SetDefault after the successful DB write, or delete the key when it returns ErrDeviceLimitReached).

TagDevice now propagates ErrDeviceLimitReached to deny an over-limit anonymous device, but tagDeviceUI (impl.go:83-95) records the device in localCache at line 87 *before* calling a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the store rejects the device with ErrDeviceLimitReached, the key is already cached, so the next request for that same device returns early at line 83 with a nil error and the device is admitted. The limit therefore only blocks the first request and is silently bypassed on retry. Fix by only setting the cache entry after CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds (move SetDefault after the store call), or by removing/not caching the key on failure.

The new authentication gate accepts retries from devices that were rejected by the limit because tagDeviceUI inserts the cache entry before CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds. At capacity, the first request with a new X-Grafana-Device-Id fails, but subsequent requests with that same ID hit the 29-minute cache and receive an anonymous identity without admission to the device store. Cache only successful admissions, and ensure concurrent requests cannot treat an in-progress admission as successful.

issues.descricao: Device tagging now runs synchronously in Authenticate, adding DB round-trips on cache-miss anonymous requests where it used to be fire-and-forget.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Anonymous.Authenticate changed from fire-and-forget goroutine TagDevice to synchronous TagDevice(ctx) that runs CountDevices + INSERT/UPDATE inline. WHY: Every cache-miss anonymous authentication now blocks on two DB round-trips in the login hot path, adding latency and DB load per request where previously auth returned immediately. HOW: Restore async tagging for the non-limit path or at least decouple denial from the hot path (e.g., async count with cached count, or only synchronously enforce when near limit).

issues.descricao: The new auth.anonymous device_limit setting has no entry in conf/defaults.ini, so the GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_DEVICE_LIMIT environment override is ignored and the limit stays 0.

comentarios.texto: The new device_limit setting is read without adding a corresponding key to conf/defaults.ini. applyEnvVariableOverrides only visits keys already present in the loaded INI and runs before readAuthSettings, so setting GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_DEVICE_LIMIT alone is ignored and leaves the limit at zero, disabling enforcement. Add an uncommented device_limit = 0 entry under auth.anonymous in defaults.ini so the standard environment override mechanism can apply it.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: After taking the write lock at line 48, the code does not check entryPointAssetsCache again, so every goroutine that saw a nil cache under the RLock rebuilds it again. WHY: When the cache is empty in non-dev mode, concurrent index and frontend-settings requests queue on the mutex and each one re-reads and re-parses assets-manifest.json in turn, even after the first one has filled the cache. HOW: After Lock(), return the cached value when it is non-nil and cfg.Env != setting.Dev.

After `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` the code never checks `entryPointAssetsCache` again. Every goroutine that saw a nil cache under the RLock therefore re-reads and re-parses the manifest and overwrites the cache, even after another goroutine has already filled it. Re-check the cache right after taking the write lock (outside Dev) and return it if it is set.

Goroutines that saw a nil cache under RLock each take the write lock in turn and reload the manifest, even after the first one has already filled the cache. If a later reload fails, it overwrites the good cached value with nil and that caller gets an error. Check entryPointAssetsCache again right after Lock() (outside Dev) and return it if it is already set.

GetWebAssets does not re-check the cache after acquiring the write lock, so concurrent callers that miss the cache under RLock may each reload the assets. This is redundant work rather than a correctness bug, and the reviewer noted it falls outside their assigned review class. Consider re-checking the cached pointer after taking the write lock (double-checked locking).

issues.descricao: GetWebAssets does not re-check the cache after acquiring the write lock, so concurrent callers that missed the cache each reload the assets manifest.
issues.textoGolden: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The exclusive lock acquired at line 48 is held (via defer on line 49) across the blocking file read / synchronous CDN HTTP request (lines 56-67) and there is no re-check of entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the lock. WHY: On a cold cache, all concurrent callers (api/index.go:82, api/frontendsettings.go:62, middleware/recovery.go:141) block on the write lock and then each sequentially re-executes the full load (file I/O or blocking http.DefaultClient.Do), producing a thundering-herd serialization and N redundant loads instead of one; in Dev mode this happens on every request since the fast path is skipped, serializing all concurrent page loads. HOW: after `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` re-check the cache (`if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`) so only the first goroutine performs the load, and drop the defer in favor of releasing the lock immediately after assigning `entryPointAssetsCache = result` to avoid holding it during I/O.
cache is not re-checked under the lock after re-acquiring write Lock, so concurrent callers can each recompute web assets

The cache is not rechecked after acquiring the write lock, so concurrent production requests that initially observe a nil cache each reload and decode the manifest even after another request has populated it. During a cold-start request burst, these redundant filesystem reads and JSON decodes execute serially under the global lock, delaying queued page and frontend-settings requests and blocking cache readers while each reload runs. After acquiring the write lock, return the populated cache when cfg.Env != setting.Dev before performing asset loading.

issues.descricao: GetWebAssets holds a global exclusive mutex through the whole manifest load, so in Dev mode, where the cache is bypassed, every request serializes behind it.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh NewTestLogger() instead of the receiver, so every log written through FromContext goes to a throwaway instance. WHY: LoggerMiddleware now always logs via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so a test that injects a TestLogger and checks InfoLogs will never see the 'Plugin Request Completed' log, and logging assertions silently stop working. HOW: return the receiver so calls stay recorded on the same fake.

This PR renames InstrumentationMiddleware to MetricsMiddleware, and no InstrumentationMiddleware remains in the package. The new test still uses the old name, so test output and `-run` filters point to a component that no longer exists. Rename the test to TestMetricsMiddleware to match the code it tests.

issues.descricao: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh TestLogger instead of the receiver, so logs written via the contextual logger are lost to assertions on the original fake.
issues.textoGolden: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh NewTestLogger instead of the receiver. WHY: LoggerMiddleware calls m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info so the write goes to a throwaway instance and assertions on the original TestLogger Calls/Message never observe it, diverging from real wrapper that preserves logger context. HOW: Return f (or a child sharing f) instead of NewTestLogger.

issues.descricao: The test function is still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware after the middleware was renamed to MetricsMiddleware.

comentarios.texto: TestInstrumentationMiddleware still carries the old name even though this PR renamed the middleware under test to MetricsMiddleware (newMetricsMiddleware/NewMetricsMiddleware) and the file to metrics_middleware_test.go. The identifier advertises the superseded "InstrumentationMiddleware" name; rename it (e.g. TestMetricsMiddleware) so the test name matches the code it exercises.
Test function still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware but it constructs and asserts MetricsMiddleware (newMetricsMiddleware). Rename to TestMetricsMiddleware to match the renamed middleware.

issues.descricao: The FromContext doc comment is copied from New() and misdescribes the method, which attaches attributes stored in the context.Context.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: The async legacy write gets its timeout context from the request ctx, which the apiserver cancels as soon as the handler returns. WHY: Legacy Create, Update, Delete and DeleteCollection calls will often fail with context canceled, so legacy storage drifts from unified storage without any error being reported. HOW: Detach from cancellation with context.WithoutCancel(ctx) before applying the 10s timeout; Update, Delete and DeleteCollection need the same change.

WHAT: Legacy.Update now gets the raw objInfo. Before this PR it got an updateWrapper holding the object that unified storage returned. WHY: Legacy recomputes the update against its own old object, using preconditions and resourceVersion meant for unified storage, so the legacy write can fail or store a different object than unified storage did. HOW: Wrap objInfo with updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: res} before calling Legacy.Update.

WHAT: When Storage.Create fails, the code records the failure with recordLegacyDuration. WHY: Unified storage failures show up in the legacy metric and are missing from the storage metric. HOW: Call recordStorageDuration instead.

WHAT: When Storage.Update fails, the code records the failure with recordLegacyDuration. WHY: Unified storage update failures are attributed to legacy storage in the metrics. HOW: Call recordStorageDuration instead.

WHAT: The goroutine that calls Legacy.DeleteCollection records its timing with recordStorageDuration. WHY: Legacy timings and errors go into the storage histogram, which skews storage metrics and hides legacy failures. HOW: Call recordLegacyDuration.

WHAT: Delete passes the object name, not options.Kind, as the name label of the storage duration histogram. WHY: Each deleted object creates a new Prometheus series, so metric cardinality and memory grow without bound. HOW: Pass options.Kind.

WHAT: Delete puts d.Log into the ctx instead of the log it just built with name, kind and method. WHY: Downstream logs from Storage.Delete and Legacy.Delete lose the request-specific fields, unlike the other methods in this file. HOW: Use klog.NewContext(ctx, log).

WHAT: legacyStoreMock and storageMock share one mock.Mock, so expectations set for legacy also match storage calls. WHY: For example, the Create error case only sets up the legacy mock, yet it passes because Storage.Create hits that shared expectation, so the tests can't detect a store being swapped or a legacy write being dropped. HOW: Use separate mock.Mock instances for legacy and storage.

In Delete, the success-path recordStorageDuration call passes `name` as the metric label instead of `kind`. This puts a resource name into a metric label. Resource names are not sensitive, so this is not a data exposure, but the label is wrong.

This test case is named "error when listing an object in the unified store is not implemented", but this PR replaced the List stub with a real Storage.List call. The case actually checks that a storage List error is passed back to the caller. The stale name misleads anyone reading test output or failures.

When d.Storage.Create fails, its timing goes to recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration. Unified-storage errors are then counted against legacy storage, and the storage error metric never sees Create failures.

When d.Storage.Update fails, its timing goes to recordLegacyDuration even though storage is what was measured. Update errors in unified storage show up as legacy errors and are missing from the storage metric.

The background goroutine times d.Legacy.DeleteCollection but records the result with recordStorageDuration. Every DeleteCollection therefore produces two storage samples and no legacy sample, so the legacy latency and error metrics are wrong.

Every other metric call passes options.Kind as the name label, but the successful Delete path passes the object name. That splits Delete metrics away from the other calls and creates an unbounded number of label values, one per deleted object.

The goroutine's timeout context is derived from the request ctx, which the apiserver cancels as soon as Create returns. This races with the background Legacy.Create, so the legacy write is often aborted and the legacy store silently drifts from unified storage. The same pattern is in Delete, Update and DeleteCollection; derive the context from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) instead.

Legacy.Update now receives the raw objInfo, so the update is re-applied to the legacy store's own old object instead of using the object Storage actually persisted (`res`). The old code wrapped it in updateWrapper so both stores got the same object. Without that, a patch can produce different results in each store and leave them inconsistent.

Mode 3 should write to Storage and then to Legacy in a background goroutine, but no test waits for that goroutine or checks that Legacy.Create, Update, Delete or DeleteCollection was called. Both store mocks also share one mock.Mock, so a call to either store matches the same expectation. If the legacy write were removed, these tests would still pass; give each store its own mock and use assert.Eventually to check that the Legacy method was called.

The case 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' only sets setupLegacyFn and leaves setupStorageFn empty. It passes only because both store mocks share one mock.Mock, so it does not exercise the storage error path it is named after. Move the failing expectation into setupStorageFn.

Previously Legacy.Update got an updateWrapper holding the object Storage actually wrote, so both stores stored the same result. Now Legacy gets the raw objInfo, which builds a new object from legacy's own old copy, so the two stores can drift apart (patches applied to a different base, different resourceVersion or metadata). To match mode1 and mode2, wrap objInfo with the object Storage returned (`res`).

The old Delete accepted apierrors.IsNotFound from unified storage and still deleted from legacy. The new code returns on any error, so an object that exists only in legacy storage can no longer be deleted through mode 3 and stays behind. Keep the NotFound case, which means re-importing apierrors.
Wrong metric label: `name` is passed as the kind argument to the metrics recorders. The reviewer noted this as outside their assigned defect class and did not formally report it.
Legacy and storage durations are swapped when recorded to the metrics recorders. The reviewer noted this as outside their assigned defect class and did not formally report it.
In Delete, `ctx` is set from `d.Log` instead of the local `log`. The reviewer noted this as outside their assigned defect class and did not formally report it.

The fire-and-forget legacy-write goroutines use contexts derived from the request context, so they may be cancelled when the request ends. The reviewer noted this as outside their assigned defect class and did not formally report it.

Some metric calls use the wrong helper (the legacy helper instead of the storage helper). The reviewer noted this but did not examine it because it was outside the cross-file scope. The file is inferred, since the analysis does not name it.

Some metric calls pass the wrong label value (name instead of kind). The reviewer noted this but did not examine it because it was outside the cross-file scope. The file is inferred, since the analysis does not name it.

Background goroutines inherit the request's context, so they may be cancelled when the request finishes. The reviewer noted this but did not examine it because it was outside the cross-file scope. The file is inferred, since the analysis does not name it.

issues.descricao: Delete puts the base d.Log instead of the enriched per-call logger into the context, so downstream logs lose name/kind/method fields.
issues.textoGolden: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

comentarios.texto: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` installs the mode-level logger instead of the request-scoped `log` built on line 96 (which carries name, kind and method) — a copy/paste error, as every other method in this file passes the composed `log`. Storage.Delete and the legacy delete goroutine therefore log without the per-request fields this PR is adding (and without the metrics method/kind context).
ctx is built with klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) instead of the enriched `log`. The delete logs then lose the name, kind and method values. Use `log`.
The Delete context uses d.Log rather than the per-call log. This is a logging-context inconsistency (not a data leak); use the per-call logger for consistency.

issues.descricao: The legacy DeleteCollection goroutine records its duration with recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, misattributing legacy latency and errors to the storage metric.
issues.textoGolden: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

comentarios.texto: The legacy DeleteCollection duration and error status are recorded in the unified-storage histogram. Every successful unified deletion therefore produces a second storage observation for a different backend, while legacy deletion failures are attributed to unified storage and no legacy observation is emitted. Call recordLegacyDuration here instead.

The timed call is d.Legacy.DeleteCollection, but its measurement is emitted using recordStorageDuration. Use recordLegacyDuration; otherwise storage receives two measurements for a successful collection deletion and legacy receives none, and legacy failures appear as storage failures.
The legacy DeleteCollection duration is recorded with recordStorageDuration, so legacy latency and errors are attributed to storage. Use recordLegacyDuration.

issues.descricao: Delete's success path records the storage metric with the object name in the kind label instead of options.Kind, creating per-object series and inconsistent labels.
issues.textoGolden: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.

comentarios.texto: The Delete success-path metric passes `name` where every other call site in this file (lines 48, 103, 113, 156, 159) passes options.Kind in the kind/name argument slot. The storage-success sample for Delete is thus labelled with the object name instead of the resource kind, breaking label consistency with the other operations and with the error sample emitted at line 103. Use options.Kind here (or insert name consistently everywhere, matching the metric's label semantics).
recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) at line 106 passes the object name in the kind label slot.

recordStorageDuration is called with the object `name` as the `kind` label: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`. Every other storage call site passes `options.Kind` (lines 73, 89, 103, 156, 159). This injects a per-object value into the kind label, corrupting the metric and giving it unbounded cardinality (one series per object name), which grows memory on every delete. Should be `options.Kind`.

issues.descricao: On storage Create/Update failure the duration is recorded with recordLegacyDuration, attributing unified-store errors to the legacy metric.

comentarios.texto: On a Storage.Create failure the code records the error with recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) — the failing subsystem is Storage, not Legacy, and it passes the storage start time. This records storage failures under the legacy metric, corrupting the dual-writer error dashboards (and contradicts the success path on line 48 which uses recordStorageDuration). Use d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).

On a Storage.Update failure the code records the error with recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage), attributing a storage failure and its storage duration to the legacy metric. This is inconsistent with the success path on line 132 (recordStorageDuration) and with mode1's semantics. Use d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).

The async goroutine performing the LEGACY DeleteCollection measures it with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). Every other legacy write in this file uses recordLegacyDuration (lines 56, 113, 140); recording it under the storage metric reports legacy latency/errors as storage latency/errors. Use d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy).

issues.descricao: Mode 3 legacy writes now run in background goroutines derived from the request context, which is cancelled when the request completes, so legacy writes can be cancelled and legacy storage falls out of sync.

comentarios.texto: The async legacy write goroutine derives its context from the request-scoped `ctx` (context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)). The apiserver cancels that context as soon as the HTTP handler returns — which is immediately after Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection return — so the goroutine's Legacy.Create can be canceled before completing, silently dropping the legacy write that this mode exists to guarantee. The same applies to the goroutines at lines 108-114, 134-141 and 161-167. Detach the async context from request cancellation (e.g. derive from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) / context.Background()) before applying the timeout.

The legacy write in Mode 3 became fire-and-forget, changing the contract callers relied on: previously Create (and, identically, Update/Delete/DeleteCollection) returned only after the LegacyStorage call had been made in-request; now it returns immediately and the write runs in a detached goroutine. Worse, the goroutine builds its context from the request-scoped `ctx` (line 51: `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`), which the API server cancels as soon as the handler returns/flushes the response — so the legacy write and its 10s timeout will typically be cancelled outright and the legacy store silently stops being updated, which is precisely what the new mode-3 integration cases assume still happens. Any detached work must be given a context not tied to the request lifetime (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or a server-lifetime context), and consumers that depended on the synchronous legacy write need to be updated.

The asynchronous legacy write derives its timeout context from the request context, which is canceled when the HTTP request finishes. Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection return before this work completes, so their legacy database operations can be canceled immediately instead of receiving the intended ten-second window. Derive the bounded background context from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) to retain request values without inheriting request cancellation.

issues.descricao: Legacy.Update now receives the original objInfo instead of a wrapper carrying the object stored in unified storage, so legacy recomputes the update and can diverge.

comentarios.texto: Legacy.Update receives the original objInfo instead of the object successfully committed to unified storage. The playlist legacy implementation calls objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old) against its own legacy object, so a patch is reapplied to potentially stale state and can persist a different result or fail rather than mirror the unified write. Pass an updateWrapper containing res, as the previous implementation did.

Legacy.Update previously received an updateWrapper containing the object returned by Storage.Update; it now receives the original objInfo. UpdatedObjectInfo can compute an update from the old object supplied by each backend (notably for patches), so evaluating it against a stale legacy object can produce a different result or reject an update that already succeeded in Storage. Preserve the canonical-result contract by passing an updateWrapper with updated: res and upstream: objInfo to the legacy consumer rather than replaying the original update against legacy state.

Legacy.Update now receives the original objInfo rather than the updateWrapper containing the object successfully committed to Storage. UpdatedObjectInfo can represent a patch/transform based on the supplied old object; replaying it against legacy's potentially different old state can persist a different result or fail, even though the authoritative update succeeded. Restore forwarding of the committed result via updateWrapper instead of recomputing the update against legacy state.

issues.descricao: The Mode 3 tests never wait for or assert the asynchronous legacy writes, and legacy and storage share one mock, so removing the legacy calls would not fail them.

comentarios.texto: The legacy half of Mode 3 is never verified, so these tests cannot catch its removal. Mode 3 is documented as writing to BOTH LegacyStorage and Storage, and the implementation performs the legacy write in a detached goroutine (`go func(){ d.Legacy.Create(...) }()`, dualwriter_mode3.go lines 50-57, and likewise at 108-114, 134-141, 161-167). Each test registers legacy expectations (`setupLegacyFn`, e.g. lines 30-32 and 40-42) but never calls `m.AssertExpectations(t)`, `AssertCalled` or `AssertNumberOfCalls`, and never waits for or observes the goroutine — no channel, no polling. Additionally `legacyStoreMock{m, l}` and `storageMock{m, s}` (lines 53-54, and the same pair in every other test function) share one `*mock.Mock`, so even a count assertion could not distinguish a legacy call from a storage call. Deleting every `d.Legacy.*` call from the implementation leaves all six tests passing, which is exactly the regression the names — and the Mode 3 contract — claim to cover.

The successful Create test never verifies the legacy write. Configuring m.On("Create", ...) does not require that expectation to be consumed, and these assertions only inspect the object returned by Storage.Create. Deleting the entire legacy-create goroutine would still pass this test. Use distinct storage and legacy mocks and synchronize on the legacy call, then assert that it completed with the intended object.

The successful Update case configures a legacy Update expectation but returns after checking only the unified-store result. It neither waits for the asynchronous legacy update nor verifies its expectation, so removing the legacy-update goroutine entirely still passes. Add explicit synchronization and verification of the legacy update (ideally with separate mocks), including the object propagated to legacy storage.

issues.descricao: The List error test case is still named 'not implemented' although List is now implemented and the case checks storage error propagation.

comentarios.texto: The test-case name "error when listing an object in the unified store is not implemented" still describes the old stub List (which returned nil, nil with a "List not implemented" log). List is now implemented at dualwriter_mode3.go:79 and delegates to Storage.List; the case merely checks that a Storage error is propagated. The name contradicts the code it now exercises — rename it, e.g. "error when listing objects in the unified store fails".

issues.descricao: The Create test case name says 'only in the unified store' although Mode 3 also writes to legacy.

comentarios.texto: The test name says creation happens "only in the unified store", but this case configures a successful Legacy.Create as well, and Mode3.Create launches that legacy write after the unified write succeeds. Rename the case to describe creation in both stores (with the legacy write asynchronous), so test output does not communicate the opposite of the mode-3 write contract.

issues.descricao: Independent per-request goroutines remove ordering between legacy writes to the same resource, so legacy can end up with an older version or a resurrected object.

comentarios.texto: Independent goroutines remove ordering between successful writes to the same resource. For example, Storage commits update A and then update B, but the legacy goroutine for B can finish before A, leaving legacy with A while Storage contains B. Likewise a delete can run before an earlier create and leave a resurrected legacy object. Preserve per-resource commit order for mirroring (including across create/update/delete), rather than launching each write independently.

issues.descricao: The storage-failure Create test registers its failing expectation via setupLegacyFn and only works because legacy and storage share one mock.

comentarios.texto: The 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' case registers the failing Create expectation only through setupLegacyFn. It passes only because legacy and storage share one mock, so the storage Create gets that error by accident. Register the expectation in setupStorageFn and use separate mocks for legacy and storage, so the test really covers a storage failure.

issues.descricao: DualWriterMode3.Delete now returns on any unified-storage error, including NotFound, before deleting from legacy, so objects that exist only in legacy can no longer be deleted.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: The new log line calls s.search.TotalDocs() after the watch goroutine has started (line 207). bleveBackend.TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without holding cacheMu, while that goroutine can write b.cache through getOrCreateIndex -> BuildIndex. WHY: a watch event for a namespace with no index during startup causes a concurrent map read/write, which Go treats as a fatal error and crashes the process. HOW: take b.cacheMu.RLock() inside TotalDocs, or compute the doc count before starting the watch goroutine.

NewResourceServer used to be a cheap constructor, and Init ran later (first request or service start). It now synchronously runs lifecycle Init, builds the full search index and starts the watcher, and returns nil plus an error if any step fails. Callers such as sql/service.go, unified/client.go, apistore/restoptions.go and dashboard/legacy_storage.go were not changed: an Init failure now aborts construction instead of only failing requests, and startup blocks until the whole index build finishes.

BuildIndex no longer holds cacheMu during the build, and getOrCreateIndex has no per-key guard, so two callers can build the same key at once and the last to finish unconditionally replaces the cached index. If the slower build listed storage before a watch event was written, its stale index overwrites the one that has the event, and that event is lost from search. Keep the per-key build serialized, or under the lock re-check the cache and keep the existing entry instead of replacing it.

issues.descricao: BuildIndex now locks only the final cache assignment, so concurrent callers for the same uncached key all build the same expensive index in parallel and the last one overwrites the others.
issues.textoGolden: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Removing the function-wide `b.cacheMu.Lock()/defer Unlock()` and keeping only the lock around `b.cache[key]=idx` removes the only thing that serialized GetIndex against an in-flight build. WHY: getOrCreateIndex (resource/search.go:287-307) does GetIndex -> if nil -> build; previously BuildIndex held the write lock for its whole body so a concurrent caller's GetIndex (RLock) blocked until the first build cached the index and then saw it (no second build). Now GetIndex can return nil while a build for the same key is still running, so two requests/watch events build the SAME key concurrently — producing two distinct index instances where the caller holding the non-cached one never observes later writes (stale search results), and, for file-backed indices (size > FileThreshold), two concurrent `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` opening the same on-disk directory. HOW: guard the build per key (e.g. re-check the cache under the write lock after acquiring it, or use a per-key single-flight/lock so only one build runs per NamespacedResource), rather than relying on a global write lock held for the entire body.

The cache mutex was moved to cover only the cache assignment, removing the serialization that previously surrounded the whole BuildIndex. Two concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key can now both construct an index (including `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` on the same on-disk path) and both write `b.cache[key]`; the second overwrites the first, so callers get distinct index instances for one key and writes made through the losing instance are invisible to readers of the cached one (and the file-backed build may collide on the same directory). Keep the build for a given key serialized (e.g. restore the lock around the build, or take a per-key lock) instead of locking only the map write.

Locking only cache publication allows concurrent requests for the same uncached key to build separate indexes and overwrite each other's cache entries. Search and handleEvent both call getOrCreateIndex, whose GetIndex previously blocked behind the build-wide lock; now an event can update one newly built index before another build replaces it, losing that update from subsequent search results and leaving the discarded index open. Serialize builds per NamespacedResource and recheck the cache after acquiring that per-key guard.

issues.descricao: The new startup log calls TotalDocs, which iterates the index cache without a lock, after the event goroutine that can add indexes has started, so a concurrent map read and write can crash the process.
issues.textoGolden: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

comentarios.texto: The newly added `s.search.TotalDocs()` call is unsafe: `bleveBackend.TotalDocs()` (pkg/storage/unified/search/bleve.go:144-150) iterates `b.cache` without holding `cacheMu`, while the bleve.go hunk in this same PR keeps `cacheMu` for the `b.cache[key] = idx` write only. Because search.go:207-213 already started the watch-event goroutine that can call `build` → `BuildIndex` → cache write, line 216 can iterate the map concurrently with that write, causing a `concurrent map iteration and map write` panic or data race. Either guard the `TotalDocs` read with `cacheMu`, or move this call to a point where no build can run concurrently.

The new startup log calls TotalDocs after launching the write-event listener, but bleveBackend.TotalDocs iterates b.cache without cacheMu.RLock. A write event for an unindexed resource can concurrently publish an index through BuildIndex, causing a map iteration/write race and potentially a fatal runtime error during initialization. Protect TotalDocs cache iteration with the same read lock used by GetIndex.

BuildIndex now writes b.cache under Lock while TotalDocs (called from search.init after the watch goroutine starts) ranges over b.cache without any lock. This can cause a concurrent map read/write fatal error. Fix by taking cacheMu.RLock in TotalDocs.

issues.descricao: NewResourceServer returns an error when Init fails without cancelling the server context created earlier.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) and, on error, returns `nil, err` without invoking the `cancel` func created at line 229 and without running any lifecycle cleanup. WHY: Init may have already started long-lived goroutines — searchSupport.init's event-consumption loop uses context.Background() (resource/search.go:202) and initWatcher starts a watcher bound to s.ctx (server.go:752-770) — so if search.init succeeds and initWatcher (or a later step) fails, the constructor discards the server while those goroutines keep running with no way to stop them, leaking the internal context and watcher goroutines. HOW: on the error path call `cancel()` (and any needed lifecycle.Stop) before returning, or defer the cancel until success.

WHAT: NewResourceServer calls s.Init(ctx) synchronously but returns nil,err without calling the cancel created for s.ctx. WHY: Failed startup leaks the server context (and any lifecycle/watch resources partially started by Init), leaving goroutines/channel watches alive. HOW: On Init error call s.cancel() (and lifecycle Stop cleanup) before returning.
