comentarios.texto: The global VIEW check returns true before evaluating client-specific VIEW permissions, bypassing a negative permission on an individual client. An administrator granted VIEW on all clients can therefore read a client explicitly excluded by a client-specific denial; ClientsResource.getClients also bypasses per-client checks when this evaluator's parameterless canView() returns true. Evaluate the specific client resource before falling back to the all-clients permission, and ensure listing does not use a global grant to skip specific denials.

Do not short-circuit resource-specific view evaluation on the global fine-grained VIEW grant. With an all-clients VIEW permission allowing an administrator and a client-specific VIEW permission denying that administrator, canView() returns true here and the specific client permission is never evaluated. This differs from the specific-over-global override behavior exercised for users in this PR and exposes the denied client's representation. Keep the administrative-role bypass separate from fine-grained grants and evaluate the client's resource before falling back to the all-clients resource; also ensure the global view result used by client listing cannot bypass those overrides.

issues.descricao: The negative check for removing a default client scope expects ForbiddenException, but it can come from the preceding getDefaultClientScopes() call, so the test passes even without a permission check on removal.

comentarios.texto: The expected ForbiddenException can come from getDefaultClientScopes(), before removeDefaultClientScope() is invoked. With no permission granted, the initial read is forbidden, so this test still passes if removal's manage-permission check is removed entirely; the later granted removal also succeeds in that broken implementation. Obtain the scope ID using the privileged realm client outside this try block, then invoke only removeDefaultClientScope() through the restricted client and assert that it is forbidden.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: configuredFor now returns true for users who only have a passkey, but only keycloak.v2/login/login-password.ftl got the passkeys macro; base/login/login-password.ftl has no webauthn form or button. WHY: In base-derived themes ("keycloak" and custom themes), a passkey-only user reaching a required PasswordForm sees a password field they cannot use and no passkey option, and the old not-configured path (setting the password required action) is skipped. HOW: Add `<@passkeys.conditionalUIData />` (and its import) to base/login/login-password.ftl so every theme that inherits it shows the passkey option.

This comment was copied from the other tests and says the block sets a passwordless policy for discoverable keys. The code below only turns passkeys off for the realm, which is the scenario this test's javadoc describes. Change the comment so it says passkeys are disabled.

After someone submits only a username, `PasswordForm.authenticate` calls `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)`. The new `authn_select` block in `passkeys.ftl` then puts that user's WebAuthn credential IDs into the page as hidden `authn_use_chk` inputs. Because the block is only rendered when the user has a passkey, any unauthenticated visitor can type a username and learn whether that account has a passkey, plus its credential IDs. Limit this to re-authentication: only fill the user-specific data when `USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH` is set, and otherwise use the user-less conditional UI data.

Missing test coverage: no test triggers a passkey failure during re-authentication, so the new `AuthenticatorUtils.setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError` call in `WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator` is never exercised. Consider adding a test where passkey authentication fails after `prompt=login` and asserting the resulting error and form state.

issues.descricao: PasswordForm now accepts passkey-only users, but only the keycloak.v2 login-password.ftl renders the passkeys conditional UI; the base template (used by the legacy keycloak theme) does not, so a passkey-only user is shown a password-only form they cannot complete.

comentarios.texto: PasswordForm.configuredFor now accepts passkey-only users even when the active login theme renders the unchanged base login-password.ftl, which contains no passkeys UI. The legacy keycloak theme inherits that template, so a user without a password reaches a password-only challenge with no way to authenticate instead of being able to use the newly accepted passkey credential. Add the passkeys import and conditionalUIData invocation to the base login-password.ftl as well as the keycloak.v2 override.

issues.descricao: The comment 'setup webauthn data when passkeys enabled' does not mention that the condition also requires a selected user to own a passkey credential.

comentarios.texto: The new comment says webauthn data is set up "when passkeys enabled", but the guard `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())` also requires that a known/already-selected user actually has a passkey credential. With realm passkeys enabled and a selected user without a passkey, `fillContextForm` is skipped (the test `passwordLogin_reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey` relies on exactly this), so the comment misdescribes the condition it documents. Rephrase it to match the code, e.g. "setup webauthn data when conditional passkeys can be used (user unknown or user has a passkey)".

issues.descricao: The test comment says it sets the passwordless policy for discoverable keys, but the updater only disables passkeys for the realm.

comentarios.texto: The comment 'set passwordless policy for discoverable keys' is stale. The updater now only calls setWebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled(Boolean.FALSE), so it disables passkeys for the realm. Change the comment to say that passkeys are disabled for the realm.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate checks the login predicate against `idpById`, which comes from getById() and is wrapped by createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel, so isEnabled() returns false whenever the linked organization is disabled. WHY: if an org-linked public IdP is set to hideOnLogin/linkOnly while its org is disabled, both checks fail, the login caches are not invalidated, and once the org is re-enabled the cached id is returned and the login page shows a hidden/link-only IdP (the bean only re-checks isEnabled). HOW: run the predicate against the unwrapped stored model (e.g. idpDelegate.getById(model.getInternalId())) instead of the org-aware wrapper.

WHAT: The cleanup is registered for an IdP with the literal alias "alias" instead of the alias actually created ("idp-alias-" + i). WHY: none of the 21 IdPs created in testCacheIDPForLogin are removed, so state leaks into later tests in the realm. HOW: capture the real alias for the cleanup.

WHAT: Adding the organization/BROKER_PUBLIC condition to the shared getLoginPredicate also changes IdentityProviderBean.federatedProviderPredicate, which the base (non-organization) login bean uses to filter the user's already-linked IdPs. WHY: when the organization feature is disabled, a user whose linked IdP still has an organizationId but is not public no longer sees that IdP on the login page, a regression unrelated to caching. HOW: keep the org condition in a separate predicate used only for cache invalidation in InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.

WHAT: Every distinct organizationId passed to getForLogin calls invalidateObject on the single per-realm/per-mode cache entry and re-adds it with all previously cached org id sets merged in. WHY: in realms with many organizations the login path triggers repeated cluster-wide invalidations, and one ever-growing cache entry is rebuilt on each new org lookup. HOW: include the organizationId in the cache key (one entry per org) instead of merging search keys into one entry.

The `LoginFilter` Javadoc says this enum holds all the fields that decide whether a provider is available for login. `getLoginPredicate()` now also checks the organization link and `BROKER_PUBLIC`, and neither is an enum value, so `getLoginSearchOptions()` does not include them. Update the Javadoc, or comment the new check, so readers know the enum is no longer the complete set.

In testCacheIDPForLogin, the cleanup passes the literal string "alias" instead of each IDP's actual alias, so the identity providers created by the test are not removed. This does not let broken behaviour pass, but the cleanup does not work. Use each IDP's alias in the cleanup.

issues.descricao: The test registers cleanup for the literal alias "alias" instead of the created IDP aliases, so the created identity providers are never cleaned up.
issues.textoGolden: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.

comentarios.texto: The cleanup registers `identityProviders().get("alias")::remove` inside the loop, and also for idp-alias-20. "alias" is a literal string rather than the actual IDP alias, so none of the created IDPs is ever cleaned up. Use the real alias (e.g. the loop's alias variable / "idp-alias-20") when registering the cleanup. As written, the 21 leaked providers can skew later tests that count IDPs or login caches.

The cleanup is registered for the literal alias "alias" rather than the IDP just created ("idp-alias-" + i). The 20 created IDPs are never removed, and the same applies to the cleanup at line 425 for "idp-alias-20". Use the actual alias, e.g. get("idp-alias-" + i)::remove, so the IDPs don't leak into other tests.

The cleanup registered here uses the literal alias "alias", but the provider just created has alias "idp-alias-" + i. The same mismatch is repeated at line 425 for "idp-alias-20". The cleanup can never find/remove the created providers (null dereference/404 on remove, or at best a silent no-op), so none of the 21 IDPs this test creates are cleaned up and the realm is left polluted for later tests. Use the actual alias, e.g. `testRealm().identityProviders().get("idp-alias-" + i)::remove` and `get("idp-alias-20")::remove`.

issues.descricao: On a partial cache miss getForLogin merges the previously read login query into a newly revisioned entry, so a concurrent invalidation can be lost and stale IDP IDs for other organizations persist.

comentarios.texto: Do not merge the previously read query into a newly revisioned entry without verifying its revision. A reader can obtain a query containing organization A's IDs, then another transaction disables a provider or changes its organization and invalidates this key. When the reader requests an uncached organization B, this branch obtains a fresh revision but copies the old A results into the new query and publishes it using the current counter. Subsequent A requests receive stale membership indefinitely (a disabled or moved provider still exists, so the null-ID fallback does not repair it). Rebuild rather than copy after invalidation, or ensure the old query's revision is still valid atomically before publishing the merged entry.

issues.descricao: Login-cache invalidation on update compares the organization-aware enabled state, so changing a broker to private while its organization is disabled skips invalidation and leaves the now-private IDP in the cached login list.

comentarios.texto: The early return compares the original IDP's organization-aware enabled state rather than the persisted enabled state used to populate the login cache. If a cached public IDP's organization is disabled and an admin changes BROKER_PUBLIC to false, the original predicate is false because the organization is disabled and the updated predicate is false because the broker is private, so the stale ID remains cached; re-enabling the organization displays the now-private broker because the login bean only rechecks isEnabled. Compare raw persisted models for login-cache invalidation, for example by loading the original through idpDelegate.getById before applying this predicate.

issues.descricao: The LoginFilter javadoc still claims its constants are all criteria for login availability although getLoginPredicate now also checks organization link and BROKER_PUBLIC.

comentarios.texto: getLoginPredicate now also filters on organization link plus the BROKER_PUBLIC config (line 254), but the enum's javadoc directly above (lines 215-217) still states that the enum "contains all fields that are considered when deciding if a provider should be available for login or not", presenting ENABLED/LINK_ONLY/HIDE_ON_LOGIN as the exhaustive criteria. Any reader — or a future LoginFilter constant added against that documented assumption — will believe organization link and BROKER_PUBLIC play no role. Update the javadoc to include the organization-link/public-broker condition, or move the condition into a documented LoginFilter constant.

issues.descricao: The login-cache test creates only public org-linked IDPs, so the new BROKER_PUBLIC check in getLoginPredicate is not covered.

comentarios.texto: Test fixture never covers the new BROKER_PUBLIC branch: all org-linked IDPs are created public, so reverting the getLoginPredicate public-check leaves all counts unchanged and the test still passes. Add at least one org-linked non-public (BROKER_PUBLIC false/missing) enabled IDP and assert it is excluded from getForLogin counts.

issues.descricao: The test never consumes or asserts getForLogin's returned providers and never repeats a query, so the cache-hit path that builds the result is untested and could return wrong IDPs without failing.

comentarios.texto: Consume and assert the results of getForLogin, including a repeat query for the same mode/organization to exercise a cache hit. All calls in this test discard the returned stream and assert only IdentityProviderListQuery contents. The implementation populates that query before reconstructing the returned models, so returning an empty stream (or the wrong providers) at line 254 would still pass the entire test. Assert the expected provider identities on both the initial query and the cached query, rather than only the internal cached count.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: fetch_error_details pairs error_ids with nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids).values() using zip, assuming the returned dict keeps input order and has the same length. WHY: get_multi removes duplicate ids and merges cached items after the service results (items.update(cache_items)), so the order and length can differ and errors end up with the wrong id or are silently dropped. HOW: look up each event by its node id instead of zipping.

WHAT: gen_request_data compares error timestamps in seconds (from nodestore event data) with rrweb event timestamps, which are millisecond integers (event_parser types the top-level timestamp as int ms). WHY: every error timestamp is numerically smaller than every breadcrumb timestamp, so all errors are emitted before the first breadcrumb and the timeline sent to Seer is not in chronological order. HOW: normalize to one unit before comparing, e.g. compare error['timestamp'] * 1000 with event['timestamp'].

WHAT: Every paginated GET now runs query_replay_instance and then a nodestore get_multi over all of the replay's error_ids, with no cap and before pagination. WHY: a replay with many errors loads every full event payload from nodestore on every page request, which adds large latency and memory use to a request that already calls Seer. HOW: cap error_ids (e.g. error_ids[:N]) before calling fetch_error_details.

WHAT: validate_timestamp and validate_age check whether the other field is truthy, so age=0 (or timestamp=0) is treated as absent. WHY: a report with both timestamp and age=0 passes validation, which defeats the stated rule that the two fields are mutually exclusive. HOW: check for key presence with `"age" in self.initial_data` and `"timestamp" in self.initial_data`.

The `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` check was added only to the search branch, while the early `return sorted;` (no search query) still returns everything. In the default view, is_segment, project_id and received are still shown, which defeats the purpose of the hidden list. Apply the hidden-attribute filter in the early-return path as well.

`get_multi` returns a dict keyed by node ID, but the code pairs `error_ids` with `events.values()` by position. If any ID is missing from the result or the order differs, each ErrorEvent gets another error's ID, title and timestamp. Look up each event by its own `node_id` instead.

`nodestore.backend.get_multi` returns a dict keyed by node_id, and its order is not guaranteed to match the input `node_ids` (cache hits and fetched items can be merged in a different order). Zipping `error_ids` with `events.values()` by position can attach one event's title, message and timestamp to another error's id. Look up each event by its node_id instead.

`validate_timestamp` and `validate_age` use `self.initial_data.get(...)`, which treats 0 as absent. A report with `age: 0` (a valid value for a freshly generated report) together with a `timestamp` therefore passes validation, and so does `timestamp: 0` with `age`. Check whether the key is present instead.

The row was changed to `max_segment_id: None` to cover the new early return in `_make_recording_filenames`, but this test patches `delete_matched_rows` and only checks that the mock received the rows. `_make_recording_filenames` never runs, so the test would still pass if the None guard were removed and `range(None + 1)` crashed. Add a direct test that calls `_make_recording_filenames(project_id, row)` with `max_segment_id=None` and asserts it returns `[]`, or stop mocking `delete_matched_rows` in this case.

`nodestore.backend.get_multi` returns a dict keyed by node_id. Its value order does not have to match `error_ids`: cache hits come before backend fetches, and missing nodes may be left out. Zipping `error_ids` with `events.values()` can therefore attach error data to the wrong event id or silently drop events. Look each event up by its own node_id instead of relying on position.

issues.descricao: The age/timestamp mutual-exclusion validators check truthiness via initial_data.get(), so a zero value is treated as absent and a report carrying both fields passes validation.
issues.textoGolden: Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.

comentarios.texto: The timestamp/age validators test truthiness and make both fields optional instead of enforcing exactly one field. Reports with both age=0 and timestamp=0, or with neither field, pass validation despite violating the stated mutually exclusive report formats. Enforce field presence and exclusivity in object-level validate using key membership rather than truthiness.

Check key presence rather than truthiness when enforcing age/timestamp mutual exclusion. Both fields permit 0, so a report with age=0 and timestamp=0 passes both validators even though both fields are present; a zero-valued counterpart also bypasses the corresponding check. Use `"age" in self.initial_data` and `"timestamp" in self.initial_data` (or object-level validation) and add zero-value tests.

Check field presence rather than truthiness when enforcing timestamp/age exclusivity. A report containing both `timestamp: 0` and `age: 0` passes both validators, despite the declared constraint that they must not coexist; with only one zero value, validation is also asymmetric. Use membership checks on initial_data (or object-level validation) and add zero-value mixed-field tests.

issues.descricao: The validation-failure warning logs the entire raw, attacker-controlled browser report instead of a redacted subset.

comentarios.texto: The new validation-failure warning logs `raw_report`, the full unvalidated report object supplied by the caller. This endpoint is public and unauthenticated (permission_classes = (), @csrf_exempt), so the payload is attacker-controlled, and browser report bodies routinely carry sensitive values (CSP blocked-uri/document-uri/script-sample, sourceFile, plus the full user_agent). Logging the raw payload on every validation failure writes potentially sensitive data into application logs; log only the report `type` (or a sanitized/redacted subset) instead of the entire raw object.

Do not attach the complete raw report to the validation warning. Browser reports contain page URLs (potentially including tokens or personal data in query strings) and arbitrary body contents. Any invalid field now causes that entire payload to be emitted at warning level, exposing it in operational logs even where the existing info-level request logging is filtered out. Log the failed field names/report type or a redacted diagnostic instead.

issues.descricao: fetch_error_details pairs error_ids positionally with nodestore get_multi values, but get_multi does not preserve input order (cached items are appended last) and drops missing nodes, so error details get attached to the wrong error IDs.
issues.textoGolden: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).

comentarios.texto: WHAT: fetch_error_details zips error_ids with events.values() instead of mapping by node_id, misaligning ids to payloads and dropping/mismatching on missing keys. WHY: assigns wrong title/message/timestamp to wrong error id and yields incorrect Seer logs. HOW: look up each node_id in the get_multi dict (e.g. dict keyed by node_id) and preserve error_ids order.

`zip(error_ids, events.values())` assumes `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` values preserve input order and that all keys exist. Dict values give no such guarantee; missing keys shorten/misalign the zip, attaching the wrong event payload to the wrong error_id. Lookup per-id: iterate node_ids/error_ids and do `events.get(node_id)` instead of zipping with `.values()`.

fetch_error_details pairs IDs to payloads with zip(error_ids, events.values()) where events is dict from nodestore get_multi. Values order need not match IDs and missing keys misalign, attaching wrong title/message to wrong error. Look up per node_id instead.

issues.descricao: The Snuba replay lookup for error IDs runs even when enable_error_context=false, adding a needless query (and failure point) to opt-out requests.

comentarios.texto: The new Snuba replay lookup executes even when enable_error_context=false. Every opt-out summary request incurs an unnecessary database round trip and can now fail on Snuba availability even though it only needs recording storage. Evaluate the flag first and perform the replay lookup only when error context is enabled.

issues.descricao: With the use-table-widget-visualization flag on, the widget renders TableWidgetVisualization with hardcoded empty columns and data instead of the query results, so every table widget shows an empty table.
issues.textoGolden: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: the `use-table-widget-visualization` branch renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />`, hardcoding empty rows and no columns instead of the actual query result. WHY: when the feature flag is enabled for an org, every table widget renders an empty table and silently drops `result.data`/`result.meta`/`columns`, a functional regression for all dashboard table widgets. HOW: build `columns`/`tableData` from the existing `result` (and `widget.queries[i].fields`/`fieldAliases`) rather than the empty placeholder objects.

In the new feature-flagged branch, TableWidgetVisualization is rendered with hardcoded empty props: columns={[]} (an empty array, which is truthy for the `columns ?? fallback` logic, so no columns are derived) and tableData={data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}. All the real result data computed above (result.data, result.meta, fields, fieldAliases, eventView) is discarded, so any organization with 'use-table-widget-visualization' enabled gets an empty table instead of the query results. Pass the actual result data/columns into the visualization (or keep the old StyledSimpleTableChart) until the widget is properly wired.

With the 'use-table-widget-visualization' feature enabled, TableWidgetVisualization is rendered with columns=[] and empty data/meta instead of result.data and result.meta. Every table widget therefore renders empty for orgs with the flag. Fix: pass tableData={{data: result.data, meta: result.meta}} and build columns from the fields.

issues.descricao: The custom cell renderers fall back to default rendering on any falsy return (0, '', null), not only undefined, so a renderer cannot render zero or an empty cell.

comentarios.texto: The documented custom-renderer contract says fallback runs when the callback returns undefined, but `if (cell)` also falls back for valid ReactNode results such as `0`, an empty string, or `null`. A caller trying to render zero or deliberately suppress a cell instead gets the default field rendering. Check `cell !== undefined` here and in the head-cell renderer so the implementation honors the advertised contract.

Use `cell !== undefined` instead of `if (cell)` to select the custom renderer result, and apply the same correction to the header renderer. The API documents undefined as the fallback sentinel, but valid ReactNode results such as numeric 0, an empty string, or null are falsy. A custom renderer returning 0 or intentionally hiding a cell with null therefore unexpectedly renders the default value instead.

issues.descricao: The attribute-keys query key no longer includes the organization slug, so two organizations with the same filters share a cache entry and switching orgs can show the previous org's attribute names.

comentarios.texto: The new attribute query key omits the organization even though its query function fetches an organization-specific endpoint. Switching organizations with identical project selections such as all projects and the same date range reuses the singleton query client's prior organization's attribute metadata, including while the new request refetches. Include organization.slug or organization.id in the query key.

Include the organization slug in this query key. The new useGetTraceItemAttributeKeys implementation fetches `/organizations/${organization.slug}/trace-items/attributes/`, but makeTraceItemAttributeKeysQueryOptions contains no organization identity. Two organizations with identical filters (particularly the default all-project selection) therefore share this cache entry. Switching organizations can display the previous organization's attribute names, and concurrently mounted consumers can reuse a request for the wrong organization. Preserve the organization-specific cache identity that the previous endpoint-based key provided.

Include the organization slug or ID in this query key. The query function fetches `/organizations/${organization.slug}/trace-items/attributes/`, but the key contains only query options. Two organizations with the same project selection (especially the all-projects selection), date range and dataset therefore share a cache entry. Switching organizations can display the previous organization's attributes, and overlapping requests can populate the shared entry with the wrong organization's result.

issues.descricao: The UseTraceItemAttributeBaseProps doc says only LOGS is supported, although the hooks are also used with SPANS.

comentarios.texto: The new shared prop documentation claims the endpoint currently supports only LOGS, but this PR also uses these hooks with TraceItemDataset.SPANS (for example in TransactionNameSearchBar). Update this comment to describe both supported datasets; as written it incorrectly tells callers that a supported and actively used input is unsupported.

issues.descricao: Error event timestamps (seconds) are compared with replay recording event timestamps (milliseconds), so errors are not interleaved chronologically with breadcrumbs.
dedupedYAxes is now just [yAxis], so its name misdescribes the code.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: The flusher processes are SpawnProcess instances (from get_context('spawn').Process), and SpawnProcess subclasses BaseProcess rather than multiprocessing.Process, so `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is always False and kill() is never called. WHY: When a process is restarted because it hung, the old process keeps running next to the new one for the same shards, which leaks processes and causes concurrent duplicate flushing; the old code always called kill(). HOW: Check against BaseProcess, or call kill() whenever the object has that method.

WHAT: Each per-process SpansBuffer.get_memory_info() calls iter_cluster_memory_usage on the same cluster-wide Redis client, so submit queries memory on every cluster node once per flusher process. WHY: Every submit now sends N times as many INFO requests across the cluster, and the totals are just duplicated (the ratio does not change). HOW: Query memory info once, through any single buffer.

WHAT: When the join deadline runs out, the loop `break`s, and terminate() is never called on the processes it has not visited yet. WHY: Those flusher processes can keep running after join returns and may keep flushing shards that have already been reassigned during a rebalance. HOW: Instead of breaking, skip the wait but still terminate each remaining process.

WHAT: The test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to a no-op, so the newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` does not wait at all. WHY: The flusher threads still race against step.join(), which sets stopped, so `(msg,) = messages` can fail intermittently. HOW: Poll until messages is non-empty (with a bounded loop) before calling join.

The docstring says the flusher creates one process per shard. In the code, the process count is min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards)) and shards are spread round-robin, so one process can serve several shards. With the CLI default of --flusher-processes=1, all shards share a single process.
Every other flusher metric added in this change tags with "shard", but spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce uses "shards". Anyone filtering or grouping by the "shard" tag will silently miss this metric.

The test only checks that the shard counts across processes add up to 4. That stays true if the round-robin mapping is broken and puts every shard in one process, leaving the others empty. Assert the exact mapping (e.g. `{0: [0, 2], 1: [1, 3]}`) or at least that every process gets a non-empty shard list.

`time.sleep` is patched to `lambda _: None` at the top of test_basic, so the `time.sleep(0.1)` meant to give the flusher threads time to process returns immediately. The test synchronises on nothing. Wait on a condition instead, e.g. poll until `messages` is non-empty with a bounded loop.

Restarting a flusher used to always kill the old process, but now it only kills if `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. That check is always false for the SpawnProcess objects created by mp_context.Process, because SpawnProcess derives from BaseProcess. So a process that hangs keeps running next to its replacement, and both write the same healthy_since/backpressure Values and flush the same shards.

When the deadline has passed, join() hits `break` before it calls `terminate()` on the processes that come later in `self.processes`. Those flusher processes keep running after join() returns. When the deadline expires, skip the wait but still terminate every remaining process.

These processes are SpawnProcess instances from get_context("spawn"), and SpawnProcess does not subclass multiprocessing.Process, so the isinstance check is always False and kill() is skipped. When a process hangs, a second flusher starts on the same shards while the first keeps running. Both drain the same Redis queues and update the same shared Values, which can produce duplicate segments and leaks a process on every restart. Check for threading.Thread instead (or use multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess) so real processes get killed.

The other per-shard flusher metrics in this change (`flusher.produce`, `segment_size_bytes`, `flusher_unhealthy`) use the tag key `shard`, but `wait_produce` uses `shards`. Dashboards or queries that filter by `shard` will not match this timer. Use the same tag key everywhere.

The processes are created with `mp_context.Process` from a spawn context, so they are `SpawnProcess` instances. `SpawnProcess` subclasses `BaseProcess`, not `multiprocessing.Process`, so this check is always false and `kill()` never runs. A hung flusher therefore keeps running while a replacement is started on the same shards; check `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)` instead.

When the deadline passes, the `break` leaves the loop before the remaining processes reach `process.terminate()`, so they are never stopped. The inner `while` already respects the deadline, so remove the early `break` and let every process reach the terminate step.

issues.descricao: The wait_produce timer is tagged with 'shards' while sibling flusher metrics use 'shard' for the same value, so per-shard dashboards miss it.
issues.textoGolden: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.

comentarios.texto: The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer is tagged with the key `"shards"`, while the other two metrics emitted in this same loop (`spans.buffer.flusher.produce` at line 185 and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` at line 195) use the key `"shard"`. All three carry the same `shard_tag` value, so this is a pure key-name disagreement: any dashboard or alert that groups/filters by the `shard` tag will silently receive no data from `wait_produce`. Rename the tag key to `"shard"` so all flusher metrics share one tag.

The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer is tagged with key `shards` while every sibling metric introduced/updated in the same method (`spans.buffer.flusher.produce`, `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes`) uses the singular key `shard`. Anything consuming this metric family by the `shard` tag (dashboards, alerts, tag-based aggregation) will silently receive no data for `wait_produce`, and per-shard breakdowns of produce latency will be incomplete. Change the tag to `tags={"shard": shard_tag}` so the tag contract matches the other flusher metrics.

The wait_produce timer tags with "shards", while the sibling metrics in the same loop use "shard" for the same value (shard_tag). Use one tag key, "shard", so queries and dashboards that group by it cover all of these metrics.

issues.descricao: The time.sleep(0.1) added to test_basic to let flusher threads process is a no-op because the test monkeypatches time.sleep.
issues.textoGolden: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The added synchronization point `time.sleep(0.1)` added after the second `step.poll()` is neutralized by the test's own `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at line 15 (same `time` module), so it does not actually wait. WHY: The comment says it 'Give[s] flusher threads time to process after drift change', but the call is a no-op, so the test still races the background flusher thread before `step.join()` and is liable to be flaky / to not exercise the intended post-drift flush path. HOW: Use a non-monkeypatched wait (e.g. capture the real sleep before patching, or use the flusher's thread/process join, or poll until `messages` is non-empty with a real timeout).

The added `time.sleep(0.1)` does not wait: line 15 of the same test does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, which replaces `sleep` on the global `time` module, so this call (and the flusher's own `time.sleep`) is a no-op. The comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change' is therefore false — the call returns instantly and provides no synchronisation, so the test does not actually wait for the flusher to process after the drift change. Either synchronise on a real condition (e.g. wait until the expected message is produced) or, if the original `time.sleep` is needed here, patch a module-scoped reference instead of the global `time.sleep`.

The added `time.sleep(0.1)` is a no-op because the test patches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None`, so nothing waits for the flusher threads before `step.join()` and the `messages` assertion. Replace it with a condition-based wait, such as polling until `messages` is non-empty with a deadline. Use the real sleep saved before patching if a delay is needed.

issues.descricao: The restart path only kills a hung flusher if it is a multiprocessing.Process, but spawn-context workers are SpawnProcess, so hung processes are never killed and a duplicate flusher is started for the same shards.
issues.textoGolden: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

comentarios.texto: The new isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard does not match the SpawnProcess instances created by self.mp_context.Process. When a worker hangs, the guard skips kill() and the replacement starts while the original worker remains alive, allowing overlapping flushing of the same shards if the original resumes and leaking hung workers. Check against multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess or self.mp_context.Process, and kill and join the old worker before replacing it.

The workers are created with get_context("spawn").Process, which produces SpawnProcess instances; these are not instances of multiprocessing.Process (the default-context Process class). Consequently this guard skips kill() for actual production workers. When a worker hangs, the replacement starts while the original remains alive and can resume flushing the same shards. Use multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess or the spawn-context Process class for the check, and fix the identical check in join() so shutdown also terminates surviving workers.

Workers created by multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process are SpawnProcess instances, not instances of the separate multiprocessing.Process class. Consequently this guard skips kill() for production workers. When a live worker exceeds max-unhealthy-seconds, the code starts a replacement and overwrites its handle while the original is still running. If the original resumes, both workers flush the same shards, and repeated hangs can exceed the configured process limit. Check against multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess (or explicitly distinguish threads) and stop the old worker before replacing it.

issues.descricao: join() breaks out of the per-process loop when the shared deadline expires, skipping termination of the remaining flusher processes and leaving them running after shutdown.
issues.textoGolden: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

comentarios.texto: join() breaks out of the worker loop when the shared deadline expires, skipping cleanup for every remaining worker. If next_step.join consumes the timeout or an earlier worker exhausts it, remaining flushers can continue running after shutdown or partition reassignment. Use the deadline only to limit waiting and still terminate and reap every remaining process.

Do not break out of worker cleanup when the join deadline expires. If the first worker consumes the timeout, the next iteration breaks before terminating that worker or any subsequent workers. They may still be blocked in Redis or producer calls despite the shared stopped flag, leaving old workers running after strategy shutdown/reassignment. Apply the deadline only to waiting, and perform termination cleanup for every worker regardless of remaining time (using a type check that recognizes spawn-context workers).
join() waits for processes sequentially against a single shared deadline and breaks without terminating remaining processes once it expires, leaking them.

issues.descricao: The SpanFlusher docstring says it creates one process per shard, but shards are distributed across at most max_processes processes.

comentarios.texto: The docstring says the flusher "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing," but the code at lines 60-66 shares shards across a capped number of processes (num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards)); each shard assigned via i % self.num_processes). With the new --flusher-processes default of 1, a single process handles every shard, so the documented contract is the opposite of the behaviour this PR introduces (confirmed by test_flusher_processes_limit, which asserts 4 shards served by 2 processes). Update the docstring to say shards are distributed across up to max_processes flusher processes.

The new docstring says this creates one process per shard, but workers are capped by max_processes and shards are distributed among them. In particular, the CLI default of 1 means all assigned shards share one process. Describe capped workers with potentially multiple shards per worker so callers do not rely on per-shard process isolation.

The docstring says the flusher 'Creates one process per shard', but the number of processes is capped by max_processes (--flusher-processes), and shards are shared across processes via i % num_processes. Reword it to say that shards are distributed across at most max_processes processes.

issues.descricao: max_processes uses a truthiness fallback, so --flusher-processes 0 silently becomes one process per shard instead of being rejected.

comentarios.texto: `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` treats a falsy value as 'not provided'. The new `--flusher-processes` click option is `type=int`, so a user can pass `0`; that legitimate-but-falsy value is discarded and the flusher silently spawns one process per shard instead of honoring the requested limit. Use an explicit None check, e.g. `self.max_processes = max_processes if max_processes is not None else len(buffer.assigned_shards)` (and validate/reject 0 upstream).

An explicit max_processes=0 is treated as an omitted limit by `or`, so passing `--flusher-processes 0` starts one process per assigned shard instead of respecting or rejecting the supplied zero limit. The CLI accepts zero as an integer and the factory forwards it unchanged. Default only when max_processes is None, and explicitly validate that supplied process limits are positive so zero cannot silently enable potentially many workers.

`max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` uses a truthiness test, so an explicit 0 is treated as 'unset' and silently expands to one process per shard. Use `max_processes if max_processes is not None else len(buffer.assigned_shards)` and reject values below 1.

issues.descricao: A negative --flusher-processes value is not validated and makes SpanFlusher construction fail with KeyError.

comentarios.texto: `flusher_processes` is not validated to be >= 1. `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` lets a negative value through (it is truthy), so `self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(...))` becomes negative and `range(self.num_processes)` is empty, leaving `process_to_shards_map` as `{}`. The following loop computes `process_index = i % self.num_processes`, which for any negative divisor is 0, so `self.process_to_shards_map[0].append(shard)` raises KeyError and the consumer fails to construct. Since `flusher_processes` is exposed as an int CLI option (`--flusher-processes`), a negative value is reachable from configuration. Guard with `max(1, self.num_processes)` / validate the input.
negative max_processes flows through `or` guard into min() -> empty map -> KeyError on i % num_processes; empty assigned_shards yields zero processes.

issues.descricao: submit() queries cluster-wide Redis memory once per flusher buffer, repeating identical INFO calls per process on every submit.

comentarios.texto: The new loop calls get_memory_info() once per flusher buffer even though SpansBuffer.get_memory_info delegates to iter_cluster_memory_usage(self.client), which fetches INFO for the entire Redis cluster regardless of assigned_shards. With P flusher processes and memory backpressure enabled, each submitted batch now performs P identical cluster-wide memory queries on the consumer thread instead of one, increasing Redis traffic and blocking ingestion. Fetch cluster memory information once from a single buffer.
submit() loop calls buffer.get_memory_info() per flusher but each call is cluster-wide from same client, repeating identical INFO N× per submit.

issues.descricao: _create_process_for_shard is added but never called.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is newly added but has no caller anywhere (grep for `_create_process_for_shard(` finds only its definition); the restart path actually used is `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`. WHY: This is dead code that indicates the intended per-shard restart wiring was left incomplete — any future caller relying on restarting only the process owning a given shard will silently do nothing, and it is confusing which restart path is authoritative. HOW: Remove `_create_process_for_shard`, or wire it into `_ensure_processes_alive` if per-shard restart was intended.

issues.descricao: test_flusher_processes_limit counts assigned shards instead of checking that each shard is assigned exactly once.

comentarios.texto: The assertion counts shard entries rather than verifying shard assignment. A broken distribution such as {0: [0, 1], 1: [0, 1]} still passes all assertions in this test while shards 2 and 3 are never flushed. Assert that the flattened mapping contains exactly the expected assigned shards, with no duplicates (and verify each worker's shard buffer uses that mapping), rather than only asserting a total of four.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once when the class is defined, so every AssignmentSource shares the module import timestamp. WHY: the `queued` value carried through the task kwargs is wrong for every assignment after process start, and nothing that uses this field to order or expire stale sync events can trust it. HOW: use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

The field is named `queued`, which suggests the time this assignment source was created or queued. However, `timezone.now()` runs once when the class is defined, so every instance carries the module import time. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` (importing `field` from dataclasses) so the value matches its name.

`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` runs once, when the class is defined, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit value carries the process's import timestamp, not the time it was queued. Every timestamp produced by from_integration is therefore stale and identical across instances. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so each instance gets its own timestamp.

The test name says it covers an empty array, but it passes `{}`, so a list input to from_dict is never tested. Either rename the test to match the empty-dict input, or pass `[]` if a non-dict input is what it should cover.

`assignment_source.to_dict()` returns `asdict(self)`, so the `queued` datetime goes into the `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async` kwargs as is. That value is not JSON-safe: Sentry's bad-pickle check (celery.py, which raises when CELERY_COMPLAIN_ABOUT_BAD_USE_OF_PICKLE is on, as in tests) and any future move to the JSON serializer will fail at enqueue. Convert `queued` to a string (e.g. isoformat) in to_dict and parse it back in from_dict.

issues.descricao: AssignmentSource.queued defaults to timezone.now() evaluated at class definition, so all instances share the import-time timestamp instead of the time they were queued.
issues.textoGolden: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` evaluates once at class-definition time so every AssignmentSource without explicit queued shares the same timestamp. WHY: queued time is wrong/stale for all later instances and defeats its purpose as a queue-time marker. HOW: use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` (with `field` import).

Field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at import so all AssignmentSources share the same timestamp. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so each instance measures its actual creation/queue time.

The dataclass field default `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated a single time when the module is imported, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit `queued` value (which is exactly what `from_integration` does, and what `from_dict` falls back to when the key is absent) shares the same frozen import-time timestamp instead of the moment the assignment was actually queued. This makes the `queued` timestamp semantically wrong/meaningless (it reflects process start, not assignment time) and would silently misreport the queue time anywhere this value is later inspected. Fix by defaulting in a factory/`__post_init__` or making the caller pass the timestamp, e.g. set `queued` inside `from_integration` (`queued=timezone.now()`), or use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

issues.descricao: The test method name test_from_dict_inalid_data has a typo; it should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
issues.textoGolden: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.

comentarios.texto: Typo in test name test_from_dict_inalid_data hides it from name-filtered runs (e.g. -k invalid_data): fix spelling to test_from_dict_invalid_data so the invalid-payload guard is actually selected and verified.

issues.descricao: test_from_dict_empty_array actually passes an empty dict, so the name does not match what the test exercises.
issues.textoGolden: Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

comentarios.texto: The test is named test_from_dict_empty_array but it passes an empty dict ({}), not an empty array; a caller reading the name will believe the empty-list/array input path is covered when it is not. Rename it to test_from_dict_empty_dict (or pass [] to actually cover the empty-array case) so the identifier agrees with the input it exercises.

test_from_dict_empty_array names an empty array but constructs an empty dict (`data: dict[str, Any] = {}`), so it only re-exercises the empty/None path and never covers empty-array input; a regression specific to that input would pass unnoticed. Pass a real empty array or rename the test to match its body.

test_from_dict_empty_array passes {} rather than an empty array. It therefore only tests missing required dictionary keys and would still pass if rejection of an array input were broken. Pass [] to exercise the named case (or rename this test to empty_dict if that is the intended contract).

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: The OAuth `state` is `pipeline.signature`, which is a static md5 of the pipeline view class names (pipeline/base.py:132-133), so every user and session gets the same value. WHY: An attacker can make a victim with an active install pipeline open `/extensions/github/setup/?code=<attacker_code>&state=9cae5e88...`; the check passes and binds the attacker's GitHub login as `github_authenticated_user`, so the new user check does nothing against CSRF. HOW: Generate a random per-pipeline nonce (e.g. `secrets.token_hex`), store it with `pipeline.bind_state('oauth_state', ...)`, send it as `state` and compare it with `constant_time_compare`.

WHAT: `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes `sender` is always present, but build_integration only sets it when `state.get("sender")` is truthy, and installation.py:44 already handles it being missing. WHY: Reinstalling an existing Integration that has no `sender` in its metadata (for example one created through the pipeline instead of the webhook) raises KeyError and returns a 500. HOW: Read it with `.get` and treat a missing sender as a verification failure.

WHAT: When no Integration row exists yet for `installation_id`, the view goes straight to `pipeline.next_step()` without comparing `github_authenticated_user` to the user who installed the app. WHY: A user can supply an `installation_id` whose installation webhook has not been processed yet, and build_integration will then link that GitHub installation to their Sentry org without checking who they are. HOW: Before continuing in the DoesNotExist branch, fetch the installation's sender/account from GitHub and compare it to `github_authenticated_user`.

WHAT: `get_user_info` calls `resp.raise_for_status()` and is not wrapped in error handling, and neither is `safe_urlopen`; only `safe_urlread` is inside the try/except. WHY: A rejected token or a GitHub API or network error during installation becomes a 500 instead of the `error()` page the popup expects, so the install dialog never gets its postMessage. HOW: Wrap the token exchange and the `get_user_info` call in try/except and return `error(request, self.active_organization)` when they fail.

`_(error_short)` wraps a variable, so the extraction step for the translation catalogs no longer finds "Invalid installation request.", "GitHub installation pending deletion." or "Github installed on another Sentry organization.". The last two were literals inside `_()` before this change, so they were extracted. As a result, the shown error text is no longer translated. Wrap each literal in `_()` where it is written (the default value and each call site), and pass the lazy string through without calling `_()` again.

`Integration.metadata` does not always contain `sender`: it is only set from the pipeline state or the installation webhook, and installation.py:44 already checks for it explicitly. When an active Integration exists without that key, `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` raises KeyError and the request returns a 500 instead of the error page. Use `.get()` and send a missing sender to `error(...)`.

`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes every Integration has a sender. build_integration (line 376) only stores sender when one is present, and installation.py guards for the missing key, so older or sender-less integrations exist. For those, this line raises an unhandled KeyError and the user sees a 500 instead of the error page, so read the key safely and return error() when it is missing.

`sender` is only saved to the metadata when it is present (line 376), and installation.py checks `"sender" not in integration.metadata`, so existing integrations may not have the key. Indexing `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` directly then raises KeyError and causes a 500 instead of returning the invalid-installation error page. Use `.get()` and treat a missing sender as a mismatch.

`metadata["sender"]` is only written when the install state has a sender (line 376, `if state.get("sender")`), and installation.py:44 already treats it as optional. Indexing `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` here without a guard raises KeyError for integrations with no stored sender, so the user gets a 500 instead of the `error()` page. Read it with `.get()` and fall back to `error()` when it is missing.

The OAuth `state` parameter, which is the CSRF token tying the GitHub callback to this pipeline, is checked against `pipeline.signature` with a plain `!=`. That comparison can leak timing information about the expected value. Use `constant_time_compare` from `django.utils.crypto` instead.

This test now sends state 'ddd023d8…', which doesn't match the pipeline signature ('9cae5e88…') used by every other flow here, and asserts only the generic 'Invalid installation request.'. OAuthLoginView returns that same default error on a state mismatch (integration.py:412-413), so the test would still pass if installation-not-found handling were broken. Use the real pipeline signature and assert an outcome that only the installation-not-found path produces, such as the 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' message.

issues.descricao: error() calls _(error_short) on a variable and callers pass plain literals, so the short error strings are no longer extractable for translation.

comentarios.texto: The helper calls `_(error_short)` on a variable, and callers pass plain string literals. The translation extractor cannot see these strings, so the short error messages sent to the user are no longer translatable; the old code wrapped the literals directly in `_()`. Mark the literals with gettext_lazy at the call sites and the default, and pass them through without wrapping again.

error_short strings bypass translation extraction: _(error_short) uses a variable so makemessages cannot collect them. Wrap literals at definition/call sites, e.g. error_short=_("Invalid installation request.") and pass _("...") literals, then use data error value directly without re-wrapping.

Translate the short-message literals at their definition/call sites instead of calling `_(error_short)` on a variable. Django's message extraction cannot extract the default `"Invalid installation request."` or the plain-string arguments at the two call sites from this dynamic gettext invocation. The existing pending-deletion and already-installed messages previously appeared directly inside `_()`; this refactor removes their extraction sites, and the new default message cannot enter translation catalogs. Use a translated default and translated arguments, then place `error_short` directly into the payload so these user-facing errors remain localizable.

issues.descricao: The org parameter of error()/get_document_origin is actually the active-organization context, not an Organization, so the name is misleading.

comentarios.texto: The parameter is named `org` but the code treats it as the pipeline's active-organization context: it dereferences `org.organization` and every caller (error() and the GitHubInstallation sites) passes `self.active_organization`, not an Organization. The name misstates the argument's type/contract — a caller following the name and passing a real Organization would hit AttributeError on `.organization`. Rename the parameter (e.g. `active_organization`) and correct the corresponding name in `error()` at line 131 so the two signatures match what is actually passed.

issues.descricao: The GitHub OAuth state is pipeline.signature, a static md5 of the pipeline view names, instead of a per-attempt random nonce, so it gives no CSRF protection.
issues.textoGolden: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

comentarios.texto: The OAuth state is pipeline.signature, which Pipeline.__init__ computes solely from pipeline view class names and therefore shares across all users and installation attempts. An attacker can obtain an OAuth code for their own GitHub account and send a callback using this known state to a victim with an active installation pipeline, binding the attacker's GitHub identity to the victim's flow instead of rejecting the forged callback. Generate a random per-attempt nonce, store it in pipeline state, and validate that nonce on the OAuth callback.

Do not use pipeline.signature as OAuth state. It is a deterministic MD5 of the pipeline identifiers, not an unpredictable nonce tied to this user's authorization attempt (the tests reuse it across users). An attacker can know the expected state and submit a callback containing a code authorized under the attacker's GitHub account, defeating the OAuth login-CSRF protection and the intended binding to the installing user. Generate a cryptographically random per-attempt state, store it in the session/pipeline, and validate and consume it on callback.

issues.descricao: The new OAuth step's token exchange and user lookup are not wrapped in error handling, so GitHub/network failures surface as 500s instead of the installation-failed page.

comentarios.texto: The token request is executed outside the try block. If GitHub's token endpoint is unavailable or the request fails with a connection/timeout error, safe_urlopen raises before the guarded response parsing is reached, and this new installation step returns an unhandled server error instead of the installation-failed response. Include the request itself in the error handling and handle the relevant transport exceptions.

WHAT: safe_urlopen token exchange and get_user_info() (which calls resp.raise_for_status()) are called with no exception handling. WHY: Any network error, timeout, or non-2xx from GitHub bubbles up as an unhandled exception and 500s the install instead of rendering the invalid-request page. HOW: Wrap the exchange plus get_user_info in try/except and return error() on failure.

safe_urlopen() and get_user_info() are called outside any try/except, so network errors, non-2xx responses, or API failures raise unhandled exceptions instead of returning error(). Wrap the token exchange + user-info fetch in try/except and return error() on failure, matching the handled missing-access_token path.

issues.descricao: When no Integration exists yet for the installation_id the pipeline advances without comparing the OAuth user to the installer, bypassing the new ownership check.

comentarios.texto: The missing Integration branch advances the pipeline without verifying that github_authenticated_user installed the supplied installation_id. When the installation webhook has not created a record, or the local record was deleted, finish_pipeline calls build_integration using app credentials and attaches the installation without checking the OAuth user's access, allowing a user with another account's installation ID to bypass the new ownership check. Fail closed until trusted installer information is available and apply the ownership check before every successful next_step.

The record-absent path advances the pipeline before checking whether the authenticated GitHub user installed this app. Installation IDs arrive from the request, and a missing Integration record (for example before the installation webhook is processed) does not establish ownership. As a result, this path can attach an installation belonging to a different GitHub user despite the new authenticity check. Verify the authenticated user's authorization for the installation before advancing in this branch too, rather than relying on the webhook-created record existing.

When no Integration row exists for the installation_id, the code calls next_step() without comparing the OAuth-authenticated GitHub user to the installer. An attacker can supply an installation_id they do not own before the installation webhook has created the row, and bypass the new verification. Do not skip the check in this branch. Either fail closed, or verify ownership another way, for example by confirming the user can access the installation through the GitHub API.

issues.descricao: The installer check indexes integration.metadata['sender']['login'] without checking that sender exists, raising KeyError for integrations created without sender metadata.
issues.textoGolden: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation

comentarios.texto: integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] is indexed without checking that "sender" exists, so an ACTIVE integration whose metadata has no sender raises KeyError (500) here. metadata["sender"] is only populated when state.get("sender") is set (integration.py:376-377), and the only writer of that state is the installation webhook (webhook.py:202-208); integrations created through the pipeline itself carry no sender (confirmed by installation.py:44 which explicitly guards `if "sender" not in integration.metadata`, and by the pipeline-created integration in test_integration.py:730-743). Previously this branch only bound state and called pipeline.next_step(), so this crash is newly introduced. Fix: guard the lookup, e.g. `if pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != (integration.metadata.get("sender") or {}).get("login"):` and decide the desired fallback when sender is absent.

`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` can raise KeyError. build_integration (line 376-377) only sets metadata["sender"] when state.get("sender") is truthy, so an existing Integration without a sender entry makes this subscripting throw an unhandled KeyError (500) instead of routing to the intended error page. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` (and treat a missing sender as a failed verification) so the mismatch/absence case returns error() rather than crashing.

The new ownership check indexes integration.metadata['sender']['login'] even though GitHubIntegrationProvider.build_integration omits sender for normal pipeline-created integrations. issues.descricao: The mock occurrence builder ignores its value argument, so tests (e.g. group_2 expected with 6 while the packet carries 10) pass regardless of which value is passed to build_occurrence_and_event_data.
issues.textoGolden: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.

comentarios.texto: The new occurrence builder accepts `value` but never incorporates or asserts it, so the occurrence tests cannot detect incorrect forwarding of the measured value to `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. For example, `test_state_results_multi_group` supplies 10 for group_2 but builds its expected occurrence with 6 and still passes. A regression that passes a constant or another group's measurement at the new production hook would therefore go unnoticed. Include the value in the mock occurrence's evidence and use the actual expected measurement, or assert the hook's arguments directly.

`build_mock_occurrence_and_event` accepts `value: int` but never uses it (the occurrence is built only from `group_key`/`new_status`), and this same helper is also the implementation of `MockDetectorStateHandler.build_occurrence_and_event_data`. Because neither the expected occurrence nor the handler output depends on the value, tests like `test_state_results_multi_group` (which incorrectly builds the group_2 occurrence with `value=6` while the packet carries `10`) and `TestEvaluate.test_dedupe` (expected built with 6 vs packet 8) pass regardless of the value actually passed into `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. If evaluation passed a wrong value, these tests would still pass, so they do not verify the value/threshold path they appear to cover. Include `value` in a field of the occurrence (or assert on it in the handler) and fix the wrong expected values so the argument is actually checked.

`build_mock_occurrence_and_event` accepts a `value: int` parameter but never uses it — the returned IssueOccurrence is derived only from `group_key` and `new_status`. Because `value` is dead, callers can pass a mismatched value with no failure: in `test_state_results_multi_group` the packet contains `group_2: 10`, but the expected occurrence for `group_2` is built with `6`. Either use `value` when constructing the occurrence so the test validates the group value, or drop the unused parameter and pass the correct value; otherwise the test silently accepts wrong group values.
